inspiration: A deliberate bite-and-hold assault behind a creeping barrage that must lift across the fortified belt exactly as the assault lands, where the prep-fire that breaks the line also wrecks the ground the assault has to cross.
skeleton: a deliberate set-piece assault must break a continuous fortified belt by walking its own timed prep-fire ahead of the advance, where the bombardment is the only thing that opens the wire and the guns but the same bombardment cratering the ground and a barrage that lifts early or late is what gets the assault killed, so the crux is choreographing fire and movement to a fixed timetable against a line built to be held in depth
title: OPERATION SLOW DAWN
situation: {TARGET_FACTION} has turned the approaches to {DISTRICT} on {WORLD} into a fortified wall. Your order is to break through it. The wall is a continuous fortified belt: barbed wire, anti-'Mech ditches, dug-in turret guns, and infantry strongpoints. It is laid out in two staggered bands across open ground that gives a 'Mech no cover taller than a fuel drum. A straight rush dies in the first band, so a rush is out. {NPC:intel-source} mapped the line to the meter from weeks of overflights. That map is {INTEL_AGE_DAYS} days old, and the enemy has dug in deeper since, but the two bands have not moved. The plan is a deliberate assault behind a creeping barrage. Your massed artillery and aerospace flight lay a moving wall of fire that walks across the belt on a fixed timetable. The assault echelon advances right behind it. Stay close enough and you reach each band before the defenders can climb out of their bunkers and man their guns. That distance is the whole problem. Fall too far behind and the defenders get the few seconds they need to man the parapet before you arrive. Press too close and your own artillery lands on your own 'Mechs. There is a second trade-off. The same fire that shreds the wire also tears up the ground. The longer the barrage sits on a band before lifting, the more that band turns to crater and mud. That is safer to cross, because the defense is dead, but slower to cross, because the ground bogs your machines down. {NPC:opfor-commander} commands the line and will fight it as designed. He holds the first band cheaply, draws your assault into the open ground between the bands, and bleeds it there. Then he throws a counterattack at any breach before you can widen it. Your force is the assault echelon at the point of main effort, the single spot where the attack's full weight is aimed. Recommended force: {FORCE_SIZE}. Keep pace with the barrage and stay tucked under it, and you are through the belt before the enemy knows where you hit. Fall behind and he is on the parapet waiting. Press ahead and your own guns kill you first.

objectives.primary: Break through both bands of the fortified belt at the point of main effort. Keep the assault echelon tucked under the barrage so it crosses each band as the fire lifts off it. Seize a lodgment past the second band, a secured foothold wide enough to pass the follow-on forces through.
objectives.secondary: Hold the breach open against the counterattack {NPC:opfor-commander} has ready. Break the belt but let the breach seal behind you, and your troops are trapped in a bulge the enemy can pinch off and destroy at his leisure.
objectives.bonus: Capture the line's fire-direction post intact, the command position that aims its artillery, with its gun-pit plot and counterattack plan. Then the next assault becomes a methodical, known reduction instead of a bombard-and-hope gamble.

complications.name: The Lifting Curtain
complications.text: The barrage runs on a clock, not on how the fight is going. It lifts off each band at a fixed minute whether the assault has kept pace or not. Stay right behind it and you cross each band before the defenders are back at their guns. Fall behind and the barrage has already moved on, leaving a manned parapet ahead of you. Press ahead and you walk into your own artillery. Once the guns open, you cannot change the timing.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Track the barrage line advancing one fortified band every stated interval (4 to 9 minutes). Assault units inside the band under fire take a friendly-fire hazard. Units one band behind the barrage face a defense that is already manned and shooting. Staying in the narrow lane just behind the lift suppresses the next band's defenders for the turn the assault enters it.

complications.name: The Churned Ground
complications.text: The same fire that tears apart the wire turns the belt to crater and mud. The longer the curtain sits over a band before lifting, the safer that band becomes to cross (because the defense is dead) but the slower it becomes to cross (because the ground is wrecked). Past a certain point, the ground itself becomes the obstacle the bombardment was meant to clear.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Each band gains one level of cratering for every interval the barrage dwells on it. Higher cratering lowers the defenders' effectiveness, but it also imposes movement penalties and bogging checks on assaulting 'Mechs and very nearly stops combat vehicles from crossing that band at all.

complications.name: The Gap Between the Bands
complications.text: The defenders do not do their killing at the wire. They do it in the open ground between the first band and the second, where they have measured the range to every meter and where an assault that has just cleared the first parapet is most strung out and least protected. The line is deliberately built to let you through the first band so it can kill you in the gap.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The gap between the two bands is pre-ranged. Units crossing it while the curtain is no longer suppressing the second band's guns draw concentrated indirect and direct fire. Crossing the gap fast, under the lift, is the only cheap way through; crossing it slowly is paid for in armor.

complications.name: The Counterattack Reserve
complications.text: {NPC:opfor-commander} holds a mobile reserve behind the second band for one job only: to hit a breach before it can be widened, while your assault is still worn down from crossing the belt. Making a breach is not the same as holding it. The breach is not secure until that reserve has been beaten back or pinned in place.
complications.mechanicalEffect: A mobile reserve company commits against the lodgment at the timeline mark (T+14:00). It strikes the shoulders of the breach to pinch it off. Holding the breach open requires either beating that reserve back or fixing it in place while the follow-on forces pass through.

decisionPoints.name: Setting the Barrage
decisionPoints.context: You set the barrage timetable before the assault steps off. Once the guns open, you cannot change it. Walk the barrage fast and you cross before the ground is churned up, but you risk outrunning your own cover. Walk it slow and the belt is pulverized, but so is the ground you have to cross. Mass everything on one narrow lane and you smash a single door wide open, but the rest of the line is free to fire down its length from the sides.

options.title: Fast Lift, Hug the Curtain
advantages: Crosses the belt before the bombardment churns the ground into a bog, so the assault keeps its speed and mobility through the breach
Gives the defenders the least time to get back to their parapets between each lift of the barrage
disadvantages: A fast lift forces the assault to keep perfect pace, or it is caught in the open with the barrage already moved on ahead
Less time on each band only suppresses the wire and the guns instead of destroying them, so survivors come back up fast behind the assault
options.consequence: If the assault keeps the pace, you get through the belt fast and still mobile, but the line is only suppressed rather than broken and the breach is shallow. The counterattack then hits an assault that crossed quickly but arrived with little weight behind it.

costs.resource: the assault must keep exact pace with the lift, or be caught in the open between the curtain ahead and a manned parapet behind
costs.risk: A unit that falls off the pace is left exposed in the gap, with the curtain already past it and the defenders back at their guns. The fastest plan is the least forgiving of error.

options.title: Slow Deliberate Walk
advantages: A long dwell on each band pulverizes the wire, the guns, and the strongpoints, so the line is genuinely broken rather than merely suppressed
The assault advances onto ground where almost nothing is left alive to man the parapet
disadvantages: The cratered belt becomes a churned bog that drains the assault's speed and grounds the combat vehicles
A slow timetable burns the entire prep-fire allocation, and it lets the enemy reserve reach the breach while the assault is still wading through the belt
options.consequence: You break the line thoroughly but cross it slowly, over ground that fights you the whole way. The breach is real, but the assault arrives on the far side late and worn down, straight into a counterattack that got there first.

costs.resource: the entire prep-fire allocation spent on dwelling over the bands, and the assault's speed spent crossing the bog that dwell creates
costs.risk: A slow crossing lets the reserve reach the breach before the assault is through it. The line is broken, but the gap closes back up in the enemy's hands.

options.title: Concentrate One Lane
advantages: Massing every gun on one narrow lane smashes a single stretch of the belt completely, both fast and deep
Lets the follow-on forces pour through one clean, deep door instead of fanning out across a wide, shallow breach
disadvantages: The rest of the line is left unsuppressed and fires down the length of the lane from both sides as the assault funnels into it
A single lane gives the counterattack reserve one obvious point and tells it exactly where to strike
options.consequence: You blow one clean, deep door, but the assault has to funnel through a lane the whole surviving line can fire into from the sides. You buy speed and depth, and pay in heavy flanking fire and a breach so obvious the enemy can find it blind.

costs.resource: all prep-fire massed on one lane, which leaves the rest of the line unsuppressed and free to fire down its length from the flanks
costs.risk: The unsuppressed flanks turn the lane into a corridor of crossfire: a deep breach punched through a wall that is still manned on either side of it

entries.event: The massed guns and the aerospace flight open fire. The curtain begins walking across the first band and the assault echelon steps off behind it.
The curtain lifts off the first band and onto the gap. The assault crosses the first parapet and enters the pre-ranged killing ground between the bands.
The curtain reaches the second band. The assault must be at the second parapet under it; arrive any later and the defense there is back at its guns.
The prep-fire allocation runs out and the guns fall silent. {NPC:opfor-commander} commits the mobile reserve against the breach.
The follow-on forces commit to the breach one way or the other. If the lodgment beyond the second band is not held and widened by now, the enemy pinches off the salient.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: The assault must be through both bands and holding the lodgment by T+22:00, when the follow-on forces commit. A breach not held and widened by then becomes a bulge that {NPC:opfor-commander} pinches off. The assault then turns into a withdrawal back across the same belt it paid so dearly to cross.

opforSketch.composition: A fortified line defended in depth. A reinforced 'Mech battalion-equivalent of mediums and heavies (45-85 tons) at Regular-to-Veteran quality holds the two bands from prepared positions, heavily stiffened by dug-in turret-class fixed guns and an armor company in hull-down positions (Vedette, Demolisher, and SRM-carrier behavior) placed to fire down the length of the gap between the bands. A separate mobile reserve of medium-to-heavy Veteran 'Mechs waits to counterattack the breach. Anti-'Mech infantry strongpoints are dug in along the bands.
opforSketch.behavior: Defense-in-depth doctrine over a prepared belt: hold the first band cheaply, draw the assault into the pre-ranged gap and kill it there, then commit the reserve against any breach before it can widen rather than feed the line in piecemeal. The fixed positions fight in place until destroyed. The mobile reserve breaks off contact at 40 percent damage, but only to re-form for another counterstroke.

forks.name: OPERATION OPEN COUNTRY
forks.trigger: Both bands are broken, the breach is held open and widened, and the follow-on forces are passing through into the open ground beyond the belt.
forks.consequence: The wall is broken and the country behind it lies open. {TARGET_FACTION} has nothing prepared between the belt and the interior of {DISTRICT}, so the order is to exploit before the enemy can build a new line. Your force drives through the breach into the open rear while the break is still fresh. The deliberate assault becomes a pursuit.

forks.name: OPERATION SECOND BARRAGE
forks.trigger: The assault fell off the timetable, or the counterattack pinched off the breach; the echelon is thrown back onto the near side of the belt, badly hurt.
forks.consequence: The line held and the assault fell back across the ground it spent the prep-fire to take. The belt is not broken, but the enemy is hurt too. The next operation is a second deliberate assault, re-planned around what this attempt learned, against a line now reinforced and a reserve that has already been committed once. The wall still stands; it is reduced the slow way or not at all.

storyElementSeed: A line of assault 'Mechs walks forward into the dust at a steady pace nobody breaks. The wall of fire crawls ahead of them, close enough to feel. On the net, a flat voice counts the lift times, even and unhurried, while the ground ahead comes apart under the guns.

is-davion.objectives.primary: Break both bands of the belt at the main-effort point, keep the assault tight under the barrage's timetable, and take a lodgment past the second band wide enough to pass the weight behind you through. Cross under the curtain, or pay for the same ground twice.

is-steiner.objectives.primary: Break the fortified belt at the chosen point, on the barrage timetable, and hold a lodgment beyond it for the follow-on echelon. The fire plan is budgeted down to the individual shell; spend it on the enemy line, not on cratering your own road through it.

inspiration: An opposed crossing of a major river: force the wet gap, seize a foothold on the far bank, and get a bridge in under fire, where the bridge is the only way to land the heavy weight and the foothold exists only to keep the engineers alive long enough to build it.
skeleton: an assault force must force a contested major river under fire, seize and hold a far-bank foothold large enough to cover the crossing sites, and get an engineered span across before the defender's mobile reserve can drive the foothold back into the water, where the assault wave crosses light and vulnerable and the whole operation hinges on the bridge the heavy weight cannot land without and the engineers cannot build under direct fire
title: OPERATION FAR BANK
situation: The advance across {WORLD} has run up against water. The river through {DISTRICT} is the last natural barrier short of the interior. It is a half-kilometer of moving water, too deep to wade and too wide to rush. {TARGET_FACTION} has pulled back behind it and blown every standing bridge for a hundred kilometers. {EMPLOYER} intends to cross anyway. The assault wave goes over light, in fast 'Mechs and amphibious armor that can swim or wade the deep channel on their own. No heavy units follow until there is a bridge. That is the whole problem. The heavy machines that actually win the battle on the far bank cannot cross until the engineers build a span, and the engineers cannot build a span under direct fire. So the wave's job is not to win the battle. Its job is to seize a foothold on the far bank deep enough that the crossing sites sit beyond the range of the defender's direct fire, then hold it while the bridge goes in. {NPC:intel-source} reads the far bank as a screening force backed by a mobile reserve kept away from the water. That reserve is a reinforced battalion of mediums and heavies, and {NPC:opfor-commander} will drive it straight at the foothold the moment he spots the crossing. He knows a wave on the far bank with no bridge can be pushed back into the river and drowned. That read is {INTEL_AGE_HOURS} hours old, and the reserve has not moved. The terrain hurts twice. The near bank is firm enough to mass your force on. The far bank is low, wet flood-plain cut by drainage channels. It carries the light wave but bogs the heavy units down anywhere off the few firm tracks. One of those tracks is exactly where the bridge must land. Recommended force: {FORCE_SIZE}. Get the wave across, hold the box around the bridge sites, and the span carries the whole army into the enemy interior. Lose the box before the bridge is done, and the wave that crossed has nowhere to go but back into the water.

objectives.primary: Force a crossing with the assault wave. Seize a far-bank foothold deep enough that the crossing sites lie beyond the defender's direct fire. Hold it until the span is across and carrying the heavy units over.
objectives.secondary: Protect the bridging site and the engineers throughout construction. A foothold that holds but a bridge wrecked on the slipway leaves the wave stranded on the far bank with no way to reinforce it.
objectives.bonus: Seize the far-bank river-road junction intact. It is the hard track that lets the heavy units, once across, drive straight into the interior of {DISTRICT} instead of bogging down in the flood-plain hunting for firm ground.

complications.name: The Light Wave Alone
complications.text: The first force across is everything the river will let cross without help: fast 'Mechs and amphibious armor, and nothing heavier. Until the bridge is finished, that wave fights the far-bank battle alone, outweighed, with the river at its back and no escape route that does not run through deep water. Every hour the bridge is not done is an hour the wave holds on its own.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The assault wave is restricted to amphibious-capable and light units until the bridge is complete. Heavy reinforcement depends entirely on the bridge clock; until the span is done, the foothold force fights at a weight disadvantage with no way to fall back across the channel.

complications.name: The Bridge Clock
complications.text: The span goes up on a build clock measured in hours (10 to 18 hours of work at a clear site), and it cannot be rushed past a certain point. Direct fire on the site stops the work entirely; even harassing indirect fire slows it. The bridge is the one thing the whole operation waits on, and it is the one thing the enemy most wants to destroy.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Track a bridge-construction clock. Direct fire into the bridging site halts construction for that turn; sustained indirect fire adds delay. The bridge is finished only once the site has been kept clear of direct fire for the required total construction time, and the heavy units cannot cross until it is finished.

complications.name: The Reserve Drives for the Water
complications.text: {NPC:opfor-commander} is not trying to defend the bank. He is waiting for the crossing to commit, then driving his mobile reserve straight at the foothold to push the light wave back into the river before the bridge can save it. His whole plan exploits the gap between when the wave crosses and when the heavy units can follow.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The mobile reserve commits against the foothold at the timeline mark (T+7:00) and pushes to reach the crossing sites with direct fire. A reserve that reaches the bank stops the bridge by fire alone, even if it cannot destroy the foothold outright. It fights to win the race against the bridge clock, not to hold ground.

complications.name: The Bogging Flood-Plain
complications.text: The far bank is low and wet, all drainage channels and soft paddy that the light wave can cross but the heavy units cannot, except along a few firm tracks. The foothold has to be drawn around those tracks, because they are the only ground the bridge's traffic can use, and that is exactly where the defender expects the box to be.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Off-track far-bank hexes are soft going: heavy 'Mechs suffer movement penalties and bogging checks, and combat vehicles are confined to roads. The firm tracks and the bridge landing are the decisive ground. The foothold must enclose them, which limits where it can be drawn.

decisionPoints.name: Where to Cross
decisionPoints.context: The river offers more than one place to put the wave across, and the choice sets the whole shape of the far-bank fight. The narrow neck is the quickest swim and the most obvious. The wide bend is a slower crossing but lands where the firm track runs. A two-point crossing splits the defender's attention, but at the cost of splitting your own wave against a reserve that can mass against either half.

options.title: Cross at the Narrow Neck
advantages: The shortest stretch of deep water, so the wave is across and formed up on the far bank fastest, with the least time spent exposed in the channel
A quick crossing reaches the far bank before the reserve can fully commit against it
disadvantages: The obvious crossing is the one the defender has screened most heavily and ranged best
The neck lands away from the firm track, so a bridge built here feeds traffic straight into the bogging flood-plain
options.consequence: You get the wave over quickly and early, but onto ground the defender has prepared and away from the firm track. The foothold is won fast, but the bridge, once built, lands the heavy units straight into mud.

costs.resource: the wave crosses fast but lands off the firm track, so the heavy units bog down as they come off the bridge
costs.risk: The screened neck meets the wave with prepared fire, and a foothold won on bad ground feeds the army into a bog on the far side

options.title: Cross at the Wide Bend
advantages: Lands the foothold astride the firm river-road track, so a bridge here carries the heavy units straight onto hard ground and into the interior
The bend is the crossing the defender screened most lightly, because he expects the obvious neck
disadvantages: A wider stretch of deep water keeps the light wave in the channel longer, slower to cross and more exposed mid-river
A slow crossing gives the reserve more time to reach the foothold before it is consolidated (firmly established)
options.consequence: You cross slower and more exposed, but you land where it matters: on the firm track the heavy units need. The gamble is whether the wave can consolidate the box before the reserve, given that the longer time in open water gives the reserve a chance to get there first.

costs.resource: the wave spends longer in the deep channel in order to land on the firm track
costs.risk: A long crossing leaves the wave strung out in the water when the reserve arrives, reaching the right ground a beat too late to hold it

options.title: Cross at Two Points
advantages: Splits the defender's screen and the reserve's attention between two footholds, neither of which he can ignore
Insures the bridge against losing one site, because the second crossing can carry the span if the first is overrun
disadvantages: Dividing the assault wave puts a half-strength force on each far bank, against a reserve that can mass against one at a time
Two bridging efforts mean two sites to protect, with the engineers spread thin across both
options.consequence: You give the defender two problems and yourself two thin footholds. Done right, the reserve cannot stop both bridges; done wrong, it destroys each half in turn before either span is finished.

costs.resource: the wave and the engineers split across two crossings, leaving each half lighter
costs.risk: A reserve that masses against one foothold at a time can break both before either bridge is finished, leaving you divided on the far bank with the river behind each half

entries.event: The assault wave enters the water. The far-bank screen opens fire, and the crossing is now identified to {NPC:opfor-commander}.
The wave reaches the far bank and begins consolidating the foothold. The engineers start the span behind it.
{NPC:opfor-commander} commits the mobile reserve toward the foothold from its position back from the water.
The reserve reaches the outer edge of the foothold and pushes to put direct fire onto the bridging site. Construction halts if it gets a clear shot.
If the site has been kept clear, the bridge is finished and the heavy units begin crossing. If the foothold has been driven in or the bridge wrecked by now, the wave is stranded on the far bank.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: The foothold must hold and the bridging site must stay clear of direct fire until the span is finished around T+18:00 and the heavy units cross. If the reserve drives the foothold back into the water, or stops the bridge before then, the wave is stranded on the far bank. The crossing becomes an extraction under fire.

opforSketch.composition: A river-line defense. A far-bank screening force of light and medium 'Mechs (30-55 tons) at Regular quality holds the crossing approaches from prepared positions, with a tracked-armor section (Vedette and SRM-carrier behavior) placed to bring direct fire onto the likely bridging sites. The decisive element is a mobile reserve of medium and heavy 'Mechs (50-80 tons) at Regular-to-Veteran quality, held back from the water and committed to drive the foothold back into the river. Neither side has amphibious capability beyond the assault wave's own.
opforSketch.behavior: Wet-gap defense doctrine: screen the bank to identify and delay the crossing, then commit the mobile reserve in a concentrated drive to reach the crossing sites and stop the bridge before the heavy units can follow. The reserve fights to win the race against the bridge clock. Above all else it pushes to put fire on the bridging site, accepting losses to keep the span from being finished, and it breaks off only once the heavy units are already across.

forks.name: OPERATION INLAND ROAD
forks.trigger: The foothold held, the bridge was finished, and the heavy units crossed onto the far bank with the river road in hand.
forks.consequence: The army is across the last water barrier and onto firm ground pointed at the interior. {TARGET_FACTION} has fallen back from the river toward the interior strongpoints of {DISTRICT}, so the order is to exploit off the bridgehead before the line solidifies. Your force drives inland from the far bank while the crossing is still open behind it. The river is forced; the interior is next.

forks.name: OPERATION BACK ACROSS
forks.trigger: The reserve drove in the foothold or wrecked the bridge; the assault wave is cut off on the far bank with the river at its back and no span.
forks.consequence: The crossing failed and the wave is stranded. The next operation is to get the surviving far-bank force back across the water under fire before the reserve destroys it against the bank: a fighting withdrawal over the same channel it assaulted across, salvaging whatever crossed. The river still holds; it is forced again later, or not at all.

storyElementSeed: Engineers wade waist-deep at the bridging site, lashing pontoon sections together under a sky lit by the far-bank firefight. Their pace never changes, whether the shooting gets closer or farther away. On the bank a sergeant watches the channel and the build at once, and says nothing about either.

is-davion.objectives.primary: Force a crossing, take a far-bank foothold deep enough to cover the crossing sites, and hold it until the bridge is in and the heavy units are across. The wave is the shield over the bridge, and the bridge is the whole crossing.

is-marik.objectives.primary: Put the assault wave across, hold the far-bank box around the bridging sites, and keep it until the span carries the heavy units over. Provincial command wants the river forced cleanly; deliver the bridgehead, not a wave drowned against the far bank.

inspiration: The investment and reduction of a fortified citadel: ring it, cut it off, and choose between a bloody storm now and a slow strangulation, against a relief that may break the siege if the besieger waits too long.
skeleton: a besieging force must invest and reduce a fortified citadel by sealing it off, then choose between an immediate costly storm of prepared works and a patient blockade that starves the garrison out, where storming spends the besieger's strength against the defence's strongest ground and starving spends time the besieger may not have because a relief force is marching to break the ring, so the crux is reading whether the place falls faster to the assault or to hunger and which clock runs out first
title: OPERATION CLOSED FIST
situation: {TARGET_FACTION} has pulled its strength on {WORLD} into the citadel at {DISTRICT} and dared {EMPLOYER} to come and take it. The place is built to be held: hardened works and prepared firing positions on commanding high ground. Its inner defense is ground the defender knows down to the centimeter and you do not. Rush it and you die. So the order is to reduce it. Ring the citadel with a continuous siege line, cut every road and supply line into it, and bring it down. There are two ways to bring down a fortress, and the whole operation turns on the choice. You can storm it: go in against the prepared works while the garrison is strong, and pay in machines for ground the defender ranged years ago. Or you can strangle it: seal it off, let the garrison eat through its supplies, and walk in once hunger does the work the guns would have cost you. The strangle is cheaper in blood but more expensive in time, and time is what you may not have. {NPC:intel-source} reports a relief column marching to break the siege from outside. If it arrives, you are caught between two attacks at once: the garrison's sortie from inside and the relief's blow from outside. That report is {INTEL_AGE_DAYS} days old, and the column is closing. The real question is which clock runs out first, the garrison's supplies or the relief's march. {NPC:opfor-commander} holds the citadel. He will conserve his strength, sortie to disrupt your siege line, and hold on for the relief he knows is coming. The terrain favors him. The approaches to the core are broken and overlooked from above, good ground for a defender and bad for an attacker. Recommended force: {FORCE_SIZE}. Seal the ring and decide how the citadel dies: by the storm that costs you blood now, or the siege that costs you time you may not be given.

objectives.primary: Ring the citadel with a continuous siege line facing inward and cut off its supply. Reduce it, by storm or by blockade, before the relief column arrives to break the siege.
objectives.secondary: Hold the siege line against the garrison's sorties throughout. A ring that lets the defender break out or get resupplied through a gap is a siege that resets to zero.
objectives.bonus: Take the citadel's stores and fortifications intact rather than fought to rubble. A fortress reduced whole becomes {EMPLOYER}'s own strongpoint on {WORLD}; one stormed to wreckage is just a ruin to garrison.

complications.name: Two Clocks
complications.text: The siege runs on two clocks you can see only dimly. The garrison's supplies count down toward the day it can no longer fight (20 to 45 days of stocks). The relief column's march counts down toward the day it arrives (18 to 40 days out). A blockade wins if the supply clock runs out first and loses if the relief clock does. You have to read both through the fog and stake the operation on your read.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Track a garrison-supply clock and a relief-arrival clock. A blockade resolves the siege if the supply clock expires first. If the relief clock expires first, the besieger is caught between the garrison and the relief, and the outcome routes toward the FAILURE fork unless the citadel was already taken.

complications.name: The Prepared Works
complications.text: The citadel's core is ground the defender has measured, ranged, and built on for the whole campaign. A storm goes in against hardened positions, guns already aimed at fixed points, and killing grounds the garrison has rehearsed. There is no cheap way through the works by direct assault, only a less expensive way and a more expensive one.
complications.mechanicalEffect: An assault into the citadel core attacks prepared positions: the defenders gain fortification and pre-ranged-fire bonuses, and the assaulting force takes losses for each line of works it reduces. A storm trades the besieger's strength for speed; the deeper the storm goes, the heavier the cost.

complications.name: The Sortie
complications.text: {NPC:opfor-commander} will not sit and starve quietly. He will sortie against the siege line with sharp local attacks meant to break a section of the ring, wreck the siege works, or punch a corridor open for resupply or escape. A besieger watching the relief road can be caught off guard by a blow from the fortress at his back.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The garrison sorties against the siege line at intervals, striking weak sections to open a gap. A sortie that breaches the ring and is not sealed before the next interval either resets the supply clock (because resupply got through) or lets part of the garrison escape. Both ease the defense and feed the FAILURE fork.

complications.name: Facing Two Ways
complications.text: If the storm or the strangle runs long enough that the relief column arrives, the besieger is caught between two attacks at once: the citadel sortieing at his back and the relief striking his front. A force fully committed to reducing the fortress has nothing left over to meet that blow when it lands.
complications.mechanicalEffect: If the relief clock expires before the citadel falls, a relief force arrives at the outer face of the siege line while the garrison sorties from within. The besieger must fight in two directions at once. A force fully engaged against the citadel is caught unprepared, which raises the FAILURE fork's threat tier.

decisionPoints.name: How the Citadel Dies
decisionPoints.context: The ring is closed and the two clocks are running. Now choose how to bring the fortress down. Storm it now, while the garrison is strong, and pay in blood for a fast result before the relief arrives. Strangle it, and bet that the garrison's hunger beats the relief's march. Or do both by halves: blockade in earnest while probing for a soft point to storm cheaply, and risk doing neither well.

options.title: Storm the Works Now
advantages: Forces a decision before the relief column can arrive, so the citadel falls or holds on your timetable, not the relief's
Hits the garrison while it is still fed and concentrated, rather than after it has had time to thin its line and prepare for a storm it knows is coming
disadvantages: Assaulting prepared works spends the besieger's strength heavily against the defense's strongest ground
A storm that stalls in the works leaves the besieger badly hurt and still besieging when the relief arrives
options.consequence: You buy a fast result with blood, racing the relief clock. If the storm carries the works, the fortress falls before the relief matters; but a stalled storm spends the army and leaves it caught between two attacks at once.

costs.resource: the besieging force's strength, spent assaulting prepared positions to beat the relief clock
costs.risk: A storm that stalls in the works leaves the army badly hurt and still outside the citadel when the relief column arrives at its back

options.title: Seal It and Starve It
advantages: Spends time instead of blood, letting the garrison's own hunger reduce it without the besieger assaulting prepared ground
Keeps the besieging force whole and concentrated, ready to meet the relief column when it comes
disadvantages: A blockade only wins if the supply clock runs out before the relief clock, a bet placed on a reading the besieger can only half-make
A long siege gives the garrison time to sortie again and again, and gives the relief time to close the distance
options.consequence: You preserve the army and stake the siege on hunger beating the relief's march. If the garrison's supplies fail first, the citadel falls cheaply; but if the relief arrives first, you are besieging a still-fed fortress with a fresh enemy force at your back.

costs.resource: siege-days spent on the blockade, racing the relief column's closing march
costs.risk: If the relief arrives before the garrison starves, the besieger is caught whole but between two attacks at once, having spent time instead of taking the place

options.title: Invest and Probe
advantages: Maintains the strangle while feeling for a soft seam in the works to storm at low cost, hedging between the two clocks
Keeps the option to switch to a full storm, or settle into a full blockade, once the relief's distance becomes clear
disadvantages: Committing fully to neither means the storm goes in piecemeal and the blockade is never quite airtight
Probing attacks hurt the force without the mass to carry the works, and a half-sealed ring leaks resupply through to the garrison
options.consequence: You try to keep both options open and risk losing both advantages. The probes cost more than they gain and the leaky ring slows the strangle. Done well, it finds the cheap seam; done poorly, it is the worst of storm and siege combined.

costs.resource: strength spent in probes and time spent on a ring never quite sealed
costs.risk: Half-storming and half-starving achieves neither: the works hold against the probes and the leaky ring keeps the garrison fed past the relief's arrival

entries.event: The siege line closes around the citadel. The last road in is cut and the garrison's supply clock starts to run.
{NPC:opfor-commander} launches his first sortie against the siege line, probing for a weak section to open a corridor.
The relief column is reported closing on the outer approaches. The besieger's two clocks both come into view, and the choice between storm and strangle bites.
The decisive phase. By now a storm must be carrying the works, or a blockade must have the garrison near collapse, before the relief arrives.
The relief column reaches the outer face of the siege line. If the citadel has not fallen, the besieger is caught between the fortress and the relief.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: The citadel must be reduced, stormed or starved, before the relief column reaches the siege line around T+24:00. If it still stands when the relief arrives, the besieger is caught between the garrison's sortie and the relief's blow. The siege becomes a two-front battle the besieging force was never arranged to fight.

opforSketch.composition: A fortified garrison plus an outside relief force. The citadel is held by a reinforced 'Mech battalion-equivalent of all weights (40-90 tons) at Regular-to-Veteran quality in prepared works, stiffened by dug-in fixed guns and fortification, with an armor element (Demolisher and SRM-carrier behavior) for sorties. The relief column is a separate mobile force of medium and heavy 'Mechs (50-80 tons) at Regular-to-Veteran quality, marching to break the ring. The two are not coordinated minute-to-minute, but they converge in time on the besieger.
opforSketch.behavior: Fortress-and-relief doctrine: the garrison conserves its strength, sorties to disrupt the siege line and open corridors for resupply or escape, and holds on for the relief it knows is coming. It fights the storm from prepared ground until destroyed in the works. The relief column drives hard for the siege line to catch the besieger between two attacks at once; it pushes to link up with the garrison rather than fight a stand-up battle along the way.

forks.name: OPERATION HELD GROUND
forks.trigger: The citadel fell (stormed or starved) before the relief arrived; the fortress is in {EMPLOYER}'s hands and the relief column finds a closed siege already decided.
forks.consequence: The strongpoint that held the interior of {WORLD} is taken, and the relief column arrives too late, to a fortress already lost. The order is to turn the citadel into {EMPLOYER}'s own anchor and meet the now-purposeless relief in the open. Your force holds the captured fortress against a relief that has nothing left to relieve. The ring closed; now it holds.

forks.name: OPERATION BROKEN RING
forks.trigger: The relief reached the siege line before the citadel fell, or a sortie broke the ring; the besieger is caught between the fortress and the relief, and the siege has come apart.
forks.consequence: The siege is broken and now the besieger is the one in danger, pressed front and rear. The next operation is to disengage the besieging force from the citadel and fight clear of the converging relief before it is destroyed against the works it could not take. The fortress holds; it is besieged again later, the hard way. The ring opens; it does not break.

storyElementSeed: From the siege line at night the citadel is a black mass with a few lights still burning in it. A quartermaster walks the works, weighing the garrison's ration days against the miles the relief column still has to march. Neither number comes out the way anyone wants.

is-kurita.objectives.primary: Ring the citadel, cut off its supply, and reduce it before the relief comes: by storm if the Dragon's timetable demands blood, by hunger if it grants time. A fortress that holds out for its relief is a fortress that must fall before the relief is ever in sight.

is-steiner.objectives.primary: Besiege the citadel, cut off its supply, and bring it down before the relief column breaks the siege. Storm or starve is a question of cost against time; reduce the place whole if you can, because a working fortress is worth more on the books than a stormed ruin.

inspiration: The relief of a besieged fortress: a relief force must break a built line of siege works from outside and link up before the garrison falls, while the besieger can turn his ring about to face the relief, so the relief has to crack a fortified line whose builder is now its defender.
skeleton: a relief force must break through a deliberate fortified siege ring from the outside and link up with a cut-off garrison before it is overrun, choosing where to breach a continuous line of contravallation the besieger can face about to defend, where the relief fights a prepared line whose builder turns to meet it and the garrison's collapse clock is shorter than a methodical breach, so the crux is reading and forcing the one seam in the ring before the place it is relieving falls
title: OPERATION OPEN HAND
situation: A {EMPLOYER} garrison is dying inside a siege ring on {WORLD}, and your force is coming for it. {TARGET_FACTION} besieged the strongpoint at {DISTRICT} weeks ago and built a proper siege around it. Not a loose cordon, but a line of works: dug-in positions and firing points that face outward as well as inward. From the same trenches the besieger can fight the garrison at his back and a relief at his front. That outward-facing line stands between your force and the garrison. {NPC:intel-source} reports the garrison all but spent, its collapse now measured in a handful of days (three to nine). That report is {INTEL_AGE_DAYS} days old, so the inside of the ring is worse than it says. There is no time for a slow, methodical reduction of the works. You have to find the one weak seam in the line, a section thinner, lower, or worse-placed than the rest, and force it fast, before the garrison falls and there is nothing left to relieve. The catch is that the besieger built this line and knows its weak points better than you do. The moment he reads where the relief is coming, he shifts strength to that section and turns the ring around to defend the works he dug to attack with. Force a breach at the wrong place and you run into the section he most wants you to hit. Force it too slowly and you meet a section he has had time to reinforce. {NPC:opfor-commander} commands the siege and will fight the relief and the garrison at once, betting he can hold the ring long enough for the strongpoint inside to die. The terrain around the ring is open and overlooked from the works. It lets the besieger watch the relief form up and pick his ground. Recommended force: {FORCE_SIZE}. Read the weak seam, force it before the garrison's last day, and link up through the gap. Hit the wrong section, or hit it too slowly, and you break your force on a line built to face both ways while the garrison behind it goes under.

objectives.primary: Break through the besieger's outward-facing siege line at a forced seam and link up with the cut-off garrison before it collapses. Open a corridor through the ring and hold it.
objectives.secondary: Keep the breached corridor open behind the link-up. A relief that punches through and is then cut off inside the ring along with the garrison has not relieved the siege; it has joined it.
objectives.bonus: Bring out or relieve the garrison's surviving heavy units intact through the corridor. A garrison brought out fighting is a force regained; a garrison overrun in place is strength {EMPLOYER} does not get back.

complications.name: The Collapse Clock
complications.text: The garrison inside the ring is down to its last strength, and the clock to its collapse runs shorter than a careful breach of a fortified line would take. Every hour the relief spends reading the ring and planning a deliberate assault is an hour the garrison may not have. The relief is forced to choose speed over method, and the line is built to punish exactly that choice.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Track a garrison-collapse clock set shorter than the time a methodical breach would need. If the corridor is not opened and the link-up made before the clock expires, the garrison is overrun and the primary objective fails no matter how much progress the relief has made against the ring.

complications.name: The Ring Faces About
complications.text: The besieger's works face both ways, and he holds a mobile reserve to thicken whichever face the relief threatens. The instant he reads where the breach is coming, he shifts strength to that section, turning the part of the line you chose into the part he most wants you to hit.
complications.mechanicalEffect: When the relief commits to a breach section, the besieger's reserve reinforces it after a delay set by how clearly the approach was signaled in advance. A breach forced fast, before the reserve shifts, meets the section as scouted; a breach developed slowly meets it reinforced.

complications.name: The Garrison Sorties
complications.text: The garrison is not just a passive prize. If it coordinates with the relief, it can sortie outward against the inner face of the ring at the breach point, catching the besieger's defenders between the relief's blow from outside and the garrison's own from inside. Uncoordinated, that sortie spends the garrison's last strength against the wrong section and achieves nothing.
complications.mechanicalEffect: If the relief signals its breach point to the garrison in time, the garrison sorties against the ring's inner face at that section, halving the besieger's effective hold there for the assault. A breach point not communicated, or shifted at the last moment, wastes the sortie and the garrison's last reserve with it.

complications.name: Open and Overlooked
complications.text: The ground outside the siege works is open and under observation from the line. The besieger watches the relief form up and choose its line of approach, and a relief that masses out in the open hands him the time he needs to turn the ring around to meet it. There is little cover in which to assemble the breaching force unseen.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Assembly areas outside the ring offer no concealment. The besieger gains advance warning of the relief's chosen approach in proportion to how massed and exposed that approach is. Feinting a breach at one section while massing against another buys delay against the reserve's shift.

decisionPoints.name: Where to Force the Ring
decisionPoints.context: The line of works runs all the way around the strongpoint, and the relief can crack it in only one place fast enough to matter. The thin section is the obvious seam and the first one the besieger will reinforce. The strong section is the last place he expects a relief and the costliest to force. A feint-and-blow splits his reserve, but at the cost of splitting your own weight against a line built to be held both ways.

options.title: Force the Thin Seam
advantages: The most lightly held section of the ring, and the fastest way through if the relief gets there before the besieger thickens it
The shortest breach to force, which leaves the most strength for the corridor and the link-up beyond it
disadvantages: The obvious seam is the first place the besieger shifts his reserve once he reads the relief's line of approach
A breach that develops a beat too slowly meets the thin section after it has been made strong
options.consequence: You go for the quickest gap and race the besieger's reserve to it. Reach the seam before he thickens it and the corridor opens fast; arrive after and you assault the section he most wanted you to choose.

costs.resource: the relief commits to the obvious seam and bets its speed against the besieger's reserve shift
costs.risk: A breach that arrives after the reserve has shifted hits a thin section made strong: the fastest gap closed up in the besieger's hand

options.title: Force the Strong Section
advantages: The last place the besieger expects a relief to strike, because his reserve is positioned to cover the obvious seams, not this one
A breach forced here, against the grain of his expectations, may meet a section he never bothered to reinforce
disadvantages: The strong section is the costliest ground in the ring to force, paid for heavily in the relief's strength
A breach that fails here spends the relief against the worst of the line while the garrison's clock keeps running
options.consequence: You strike where you are least expected and most opposed. Surprise may carry a section the besieger left strong by default and never reinforced, but the cost of forcing it is the highest in the ring, and a failure spends the relief for nothing.

costs.resource: the relief's strength, spent forcing the heaviest section of the line for the sake of surprise
costs.risk: A failed assault on the strong section breaks the relief against the worst of the ring while the garrison dies behind it

options.title: Feint Wide, Blow Narrow
advantages: A demonstration at one section pulls the besieger's reserve toward it while the real breach goes in somewhere else
Splits the besieger's attention across the ring, buying time against the reserve's shift to the true breach point
disadvantages: Dividing the relief between the feint and the breach leaves the real assault lighter against the line
A besieger who sees the feint for what it is shifts to the true breach anyway and meets a divided relief
options.consequence: You buy delay against the besieger's reserve by giving him two threats, at the cost of a lighter true breach. Sold well, the corridor opens before he recovers; seen through, the divided relief is too thin at the one section that matters.

costs.resource: the relief split between the feint and the true breach, leaving it lighter at the decisive point
costs.risk: A besieger who sees through the feint reinforces the true breach and meets a divided, weakened relief at the one section that counts

entries.event: The relief force closes on the outer approaches to the siege ring. The besieger's outward-facing line mans its positions and watches the relief begin to form up.
The relief commits to its breach section. {NPC:opfor-commander} begins shifting his reserve to thicken the threatened face.
The assault on the ring goes in. If it is coordinated, the garrison sorties against the inner face of the same section.
The garrison's collapse clock nears its end. The corridor must be open and the link-up made before the strongpoint inside falls.
The corridor is open and held, or the garrison is overrun and the relief is left assaulting a ring with nothing left inside it to save.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: The relief must breach the ring, link up, and open a held corridor before the garrison-collapse clock expires around T+20:00. If the strongpoint falls first, the relief has spent its strength on a fortified line to reach a garrison that is already gone. The operation then becomes a fighting withdrawal from inside the ring.

opforSketch.composition: A besieging force fighting both ways. A reinforced 'Mech battalion-equivalent of mediums and heavies (45-80 tons) at Regular-to-Veteran quality holds the outward-facing siege line from prepared works, stiffened by dug-in fixed guns and an armor company (Vedette and Demolisher behavior) in the siege works, with a mobile 'Mech reserve held back to thicken whichever face the relief threatens. The weakened garrison force inside the ring is a potential ally, not an enemy.
opforSketch.behavior: Siege-line defense facing both ways: hold the ring against both the garrison at the back and the relief at the front, shift the mobile reserve to reinforce the threatened section as soon as the relief's line of approach is read, and bet on holding the line long enough for the garrison inside to collapse on its own clock. The line fights from prepared positions until destroyed; the reserve maneuvers to seal any breach before the corridor can be opened and held.

forks.name: OPERATION JOINED HANDS
forks.trigger: The ring was breached, the corridor opened and held, and the relief linked up with the garrison before it fell.
forks.consequence: The siege is broken from the outside and the garrison is saved. The besieger's ring is split, and now his force is the one in danger of being caught between the relieved strongpoint and the relief. The order is to hold the opened corridor and the strongpoint together and turn the broken siege into a counterstroke. Your force anchors the link-up while the besieger decides whether to fight or fall back. The hand is open; now it closes its grip.

forks.name: OPERATION EMPTY CORRIDOR
forks.trigger: The garrison fell before the corridor opened, or the relief was broken against the ring; the strongpoint is lost and the relief is spent at the wrong section.
forks.consequence: The relief came too late, or at too high a cost, and the garrison is gone. The next operation is to disengage the relief force from the siege works it could not force and pull it clear before the besieger, freed of the strongpoint, turns his whole strength on it. The ring held; the strongpoint is retaken later, if at all. The hand closes empty; it does not break.

storyElementSeed: A signals tech works a tight directional beam toward the dying strongpoint inside the ring. He is trying to tell the garrison which section the relief will hit, so the sortie lands in the right place. Then he waits through a long silence for the two flashes that will mean they heard.

is-davion.objectives.primary: Break the besieger's ring at the right seam and link up with the cut-off garrison before it collapses, opening a corridor and holding it. Read the line fast and force it faster, because the garrison's clock is shorter than a careful breach would take.

is-marik.objectives.primary: Force the siege ring at the section you can crack in time, reach the garrison before it falls, then hold the corridor open. Command wants the strongpoint relieved, not a relief force broken on a line built to face both ways.

inspiration: Closing the pocket: two pincers race to meet and seal a withdrawing enemy field force before it escapes through the closing gap, where the enemy fights outward to keep the corridor open and the attacker must close the jaw against everything trying to get out.
skeleton: an encircling force must close the last gap of a pocket on a withdrawing enemy field force, driving one pincer to a link-up with the other while the trapped enemy fights outward with everything it has to keep the escape corridor open, where sealing the gap traps a whole force but the closing jaw is hit from inside by an enemy with nothing to lose and from outside by a relief trying to reopen the neck, so the crux is closing and holding a seam against pressure from both sides before the pocket drains
title: OPERATION CLOSING JAW
situation: {TARGET_FACTION}'s field force on {WORLD} is beaten and running, and {EMPLOYER} means to make sure it does not run far. The enemy's main strength in {DISTRICT} has been driven into a bulge in the line, with two of your columns converging to pinch off its base. A whole force, battalions and not companies, is funneling back through a single narrowing neck of ground toward the one open road still leading out. Close that neck and the entire force in the pocket is trapped, to be destroyed or captured at your leisure. Leave it open and the enemy escapes to fight again on better ground. Your force drives one of the two pincers to the link-up that seals the pocket. The other pincer closes from the far side. The gap between them is the neck, and it is shrinking by the hour. {NPC:intel-source} reads the pocket draining fast. The trapped force pours through the neck in whatever order it can manage, abandons what it cannot move, and fights outward at the shoulders to keep the corridor open. That read is {INTEL_AGE_HOURS} hours old, and the flow is heaviest at the neck itself. The closing jaw is the hardest place on the battlefield. From inside, the trapped force throws everything it has against the pincers to keep the gap open. It is an enemy with nothing left to lose, fighting to break out. From outside, a relief force may strike the neck to pry it back open and drain more of the pocket. Your pincer has to reach the link-up and then hold the seam against both pressures at once, in the window after the gap closes but before it is firmly sealed. {NPC:opfor-commander} commands the breakout and will spend the rear of his force to save the front, fighting outward at the shoulders to buy the escape road a few more hours. The ground is open and fast. Good country for the race to the link-up, and bad country for a thin seam pressed from both sides. Recommended force: {FORCE_SIZE}. Close the jaw, meet the other pincer, and hold the seam shut until the pocket is sealed. Reach the neck too slowly, or hold it too thin, and the force you cornered is gone up the road before the gap can close.

objectives.primary: Drive the pincer to the link-up with the converging force and close the neck of the pocket. Hold the sealed seam shut until the trapped enemy field force can be reduced inside it.
objectives.secondary: Hold the seam against the breakout from inside and any relief from outside, both at once. A gap closed and then reopened drains the pocket and undoes the whole encirclement.
objectives.bonus: Capture the trapped force's heavy units and supply intact rather than letting them be destroyed or escape. A field force captured whole is strength denied to {TARGET_FACTION} for the rest of the campaign, not merely beaten back.

complications.name: The Draining Pocket
complications.text: The neck is open and the trapped force is pouring through it. Every hour the gap stays open, more of the pocket escapes up the road, and the prize shrinks from a whole force down to a rearguard. The race to the link-up is a race against this drain: close the neck fast and trap everything, close it slowly and trap only what could not run quick enough.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Track a pocket-drain clock from the start (the pocket takes 8 to 18 hours to fully drain). Each interval the neck stays open, a portion of the trapped force escapes, which reduces the prize and lowers the value of a SUCCESS. Closing the link-up early traps the maximum force; closing it late traps only the rearguard.

complications.name: Breakout from Inside
complications.text: The trapped force fights outward at the shoulders of the neck with the desperation of men who know what a sealed pocket means. As your pincer closes the gap, it is struck from inside by everything the enemy can turn around: a breakout attack aimed at keeping the corridor open, pressed hardest exactly where the jaw is about to shut.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The trapped force attacks the closing pincer from inside the pocket, concentrating against the link-up point. The breakout presses hardest as the gap narrows. A seam held thin at the moment of closing can be torn back open from within, which resets the drain clock.

complications.name: The Relief at the Neck
complications.text: From outside the pocket, a relief force may drive at the neck to pry it back open from the far side, catching your closing pincer between the breakout from within and the relief from without. The seam is most vulnerable in the hour after it closes, before it can be reinforced into a real line.
complications.mechanicalEffect: At the relief's arrival mark, an outside force strikes the sealed seam from beyond the pocket while the breakout presses from within. The pincer holds the seam in two directions at once. A seam not reinforced before these two attacks converge can be reopened, and the FAILURE fork's threat rises.

complications.name: Open and Fast Both Ways
complications.text: The country is open and quick, which speeds your pincer to the link-up but speeds the trapped force up the road just as well. The same ground that lets you race to close the jaw lets the enemy race to drain through it, and a thin seam on open ground can be turned in a single fast stroke from either side.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Open terrain speeds movement for both sides equally: the pincer reaches the link-up faster, but the drain runs faster too, and the seam, once closed, has little terrain to anchor on. Holding it requires depth that the open ground does not provide for free.

decisionPoints.name: Closing the Neck
decisionPoints.context: The pincer is driving for the link-up and the gap is shrinking. You can race straight for the neck and seal it at the earliest possible moment, thin but fast. You can close deliberately and arrive at the seam already strong enough to hold both ways. Or you can let the front of the pocket run and cut the neck behind it, trapping the rear and the heavy units while the lead escapes. Each choice traps a different prize and holds a different seam.

options.title: Race to Seal Now
advantages: Closes the neck at the earliest possible hour, trapping the largest share of the pocket before it can drain away
Denies the trapped force the time to organize its breakout against a seam that is still forming
disadvantages: A pincer that races to the link-up arrives thin, with no depth behind the seam
A thin seam at the moment of closing is the easiest to tear open, caught by the breakout from inside and the relief from outside at once
options.consequence: You trap the most by closing fast, but you hold the seam with a thin line that the breakout and the relief together may tear back open: the largest prize behind the most fragile lock.

costs.resource: the pincer races forward thin, with no depth behind the sealed seam
costs.risk: A thin seam at the instant of closing is torn open by the breakout and the relief together, and the pocket drains through the gap you just shut

options.title: Close Deliberately, Hold Strong
advantages: Arrives at the link-up with depth behind the seam: a lock built to hold against pressure from both sides
A strong seam resists both the breakout and the relief, and stays shut once it is closed
disadvantages: A deliberate advance is a slower advance, so more of the pocket drains up the road before the gap closes
The deliberate pincer traps a smaller force, because it gave the lead elements time to escape
options.consequence: You hold the seam shut for certain, but you close it on a pocket that has already partly drained. The lock is solid and the prize inside it smaller: you trap what is left, and you trap it for good.

costs.resource: every hour a deliberate advance spends is an hour the pocket drains up the road
costs.risk: A seam closed strong but late shuts on a half-empty pocket: a solid lock on a prize that has mostly already gotten away

options.title: Cut Behind the Lead
advantages: Lets the pocket's lead elements run and cuts the neck behind them, trapping the rear, the heavy units, and the supply that could not move fast
Cuts where the trapped force is heaviest and least mobile, taking the real combat strength rather than the runners
disadvantages: The escaped lead elements are now behind your pincer's deep flank, free to turn and strike the seam from outside alongside the relief
Cutting deep behind the lead exposes the pincer to being caught between the trapped rear and the escaped front
options.consequence: You trade the runners for the heavy combat strength, sealing the rear of the pocket where the prize is richest. But the elements you let run are loose behind you, and the seam is now pressed by the trapped rear and the escaped lead at once.

costs.resource: the pincer cuts deep behind the lead, exposing its own flank to the elements it let escape
costs.risk: The escaped lead turns on the pincer's rear while the trapped force presses its front: caught between the part of the pocket you took and the part you let go

entries.event: The pincer begins its drive for the link-up. The trapped force, seeing the jaws closing, speeds up its withdrawal through the neck.
The pocket drains hardest as the trapped force pours up the road. The neck narrows toward the link-up point.
The pincers near the link-up. {NPC:opfor-commander} turns his rearguard to attack the closing seam from inside the pocket.
A relief force strikes the neck from outside to pry it open. The seam, if closed, is now pressed from both sides at once.
The pocket is sealed and the seam holds, or the gap is reopened and the trapped force drains through onto the open road.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: The neck must be closed and the seam held against both the breakout and the relief by T+20:00, before the pocket drains. A seam reopened, or never closed, lets the trapped force escape up the road. The encirclement then becomes a pursuit of a force that got away.

opforSketch.composition: A withdrawing field force fighting to break out. A battalion-plus of all-weight 'Mechs (35-90 tons) at Regular quality, disorganized by the withdrawal but numerous, fights outward at the shoulders of the neck with whatever can be turned around, supported by a mobile armor element (Manticore and SRM-carrier behavior) covering the road. A separate outside relief force of medium 'Mechs at Regular-to-Veteran quality may strike the neck from beyond the pocket. The trapped force fights with the desperation of the cornered.
opforSketch.behavior: Breakout doctrine under encirclement: spend the rearguard to keep the corridor open, attack the closing pincer from inside the pocket with everything that can be massed at the neck, and pour the rest of the force up the road while the gap holds. The breakout presses hardest at the moment of closing, and the outside relief drives for the seam to reopen it. The trapped force does not hold ground; it fights only to keep the road open and drain through it.

forks.name: OPERATION REDUCED POCKET
forks.trigger: The neck was closed, the seam held against both pressures, and the trapped force is sealed inside the pocket.
forks.consequence: A whole enemy field force is trapped on {WORLD} with no way out, and the campaign turns on its destruction. The order is to compress and destroy the sealed pocket before it can organize a coordinated breakout from within. Your force holds the seam and tightens the ring while the trapped strength is broken up. The jaw closed; now it grinds.

forks.name: OPERATION OPEN ROAD
forks.trigger: The seam was torn open, or never closed in time; the trapped force drained through the neck onto the open road and escaped.
forks.consequence: The pocket leaked and the enemy got out: beaten, but intact enough to reform on ground of his own choosing. The next operation is a pursuit, chasing the escaped force up the open road to catch it before it can dig in again, on terms far worse than a sealed pocket would have given. The jaw missed; the chase is on. The encirclement turns into a hunt.

storyElementSeed: At the link-up point, two recon elements from the converging pincers find each other across a field in the half-light and trade a recognition signal. Nobody cheers. They are already turning outward to face the road, still full of an enemy that has not stopped coming.

is-davion.objectives.primary: Drive the pincer to the link-up, close the neck on the withdrawing force, and hold the seam shut against the breakout and any relief. Reach the neck fast and you trap the whole force; reach it slow and you trap only the rearguard, but either way close the jaw.

is-steiner.objectives.primary: Close the pocket at the link-up and hold the seam against pressure from both sides until the trapped force is sealed. A field force taken whole is worth more than one beaten and let run, so close the jaw before the pocket drains.

POCKET_DRAIN_HOURS.unit: hours for the pocket to drain

inspiration: Breakthrough and exploitation: crack the defensive crust at a chosen point and pour through into the open rear before the enemy's mobile reserve can reseal the penetration, where every hour spent widening the shoulders is an hour the gap stays open and an hour not spent driving deep.
skeleton: a breakthrough force must punch a clean penetration through a defensive crust at the chosen point and exploit into the open rear before the defender's mobile reserve reseals the gap behind it, where the penetration is shallow and reversible until the shoulders are secured but every unit spent widening the shoulders is a unit not driving deep, so the crux is the race between exploiting the gap and the reserve closing it, and whether to widen or to drive
title: OPERATION FAST WATER
situation: The deliberate fighting on {WORLD} has cracked {TARGET_FACTION}'s line at one point, and {EMPLOYER} means to turn that crack into a flood. The defensive crust across {DISTRICT} has been broken at a single seam. A narrow penetration is punched through the forward positions, with open country beyond it and nothing prepared between the crust and the enemy's deep rear. Your force is the exploitation echelon, held back fresh and fast for exactly this moment. Pour through the gap before it closes, drive into the undefended depth, cut the roads, overrun the supply, and unhinge the whole line from behind. The penetration is everything, and it will not last. Right now it is shallow and reversible, held open only at the point of the break, with the defender's positions still intact on both shoulders, the sides of the gap. {NPC:intel-source} reports the enemy's mobile reserve already moving to reseal it. It is a concentrated force driving for the shoulders to pinch the gap shut behind whatever has gone through. That read is {INTEL_AGE_HOURS} hours old, and the reserve is closing. That sets the whole problem. Every hour spent widening the shoulders, beating the defender's positions back on either side to make the gap permanent, is an hour the exploitation is not driving deep while the rear is still soft. And every unit sent deep is a unit not holding the shoulders open behind it. Drive too deep too fast and the reserve closes the gap behind you, trapping the exploitation in the enemy depth with the crust resealed at its back. Widen too long and the rear hardens before you can reach it, and the breakthrough achieves nothing but a wider dent in a line that never actually broke. {NPC:opfor-commander} commands the reserve and will not fight for the depth. He drives straight for the shoulders to cut the penetration off at its root, betting he can seal the crust faster than you can make the gap permanent. The country beyond the crust is open and fast, made for exploitation and just as good for a reserve racing to close a gap. Recommended force: {FORCE_SIZE}. Pour through, choose between widening the shoulders and driving deep, and turn the crack into a collapse. Get the balance wrong and the gap closes on the wrong side of your force.

objectives.primary: Exploit the penetration through the defensive crust, driving into the enemy's open rear to cut its supply roads and unhinge the line, before the mobile reserve reseals the gap behind you.
objectives.secondary: Keep the shoulders of the penetration open behind the exploitation. A force that drives deep and is then cut off by a resealed gap has not exploited the breakthrough; it has been swallowed by it.
objectives.bonus: Overrun the line's rear supply dumps and command posts intact during the drive. This is the difference between unhinging the defense for a day and collapsing it for the rest of the campaign.

complications.name: The Reseal Clock
complications.text: The penetration is open now but closing later. The defender's reserve is driving for the shoulders of the gap, and from the moment it arrives the crust begins to weld shut behind anything that has gone through. The exploitation is racing a clock it cannot see precisely: the hour the gap closes is the hour everything in the rear is cut off.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Track a reseal clock counting down to the reserve's arrival at the gap's shoulders (5 to 12 hours). Once the reserve reaches the shoulders, the gap begins closing unless the shoulders are held. Exploitation units beyond a closed gap are cut off, lose reinforcement and resupply, and feed the FAILURE fork.

complications.name: Widen or Drive
complications.text: There is one force and two jobs. The shoulders of the gap must be widened and held to keep the penetration permanent. The depth must be driven to make the breakthrough mean anything. Every machine doing one job is a machine not doing the other, and there is not enough force to do both fully against the clock.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Force committed to widening the shoulders is unavailable for the deep drive, and vice versa. Widening slows the reseal clock and secures the gap but reduces the depth reached. Driving deep maximizes the exploitation's reach but leaves the shoulders thin and the gap quicker to close.

complications.name: Soft Rear, Hardening
complications.text: The enemy's rear is soft right now: supply columns, repair parks, command posts, none of it arranged to fight an exploitation that should never have gotten through. But it hardens by the hour as the defender scrapes together blocking forces from whatever is back there. The deepest prizes are richest now and better defended later.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Rear objectives are lightly held early and steadily reinforced as the engagement runs. Reaching a deep target early overruns it cheaply; reaching it late means meeting a hastily assembled blocking force, and the bonus objective's value decays the longer the exploitation takes to arrive.

complications.name: The Reserve Goes for the Root
complications.text: {NPC:opfor-commander} will not chase the exploitation into the depth; he knows that is a fight he loses. He drives straight for the shoulders of the gap to cut the penetration off at its root, betting that sealing the crust behind the exploitation kills it more surely than meeting it head-on ever could.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The reserve ignores the deep exploitation and concentrates entirely on the gap's shoulders. It fights to seal the penetration rather than defend the rear. A force that races deep without holding the shoulders finds the reserve closing the gap behind it while it is far away and unable to return in time.

decisionPoints.name: Widen or Drive
decisionPoints.context: The exploitation is through the gap and the reserve is coming for the shoulders. You can throw weight onto the shoulders to widen and hold the penetration before driving deep: secure the gap first, then exploit. You can drive everything deep at once and race the reseal clock: reach the rear before it hardens and before the gap closes. Or you can split the force, holding the shoulders with one part while the other drives, and risk both being too light.

options.title: Widen the Shoulders First
advantages: Beats the defender's positions back on both sides of the gap, making the penetration permanent before exploiting it
Holds the crust open so the exploitation, once it drives, has a secured road home and a clear line of supply
disadvantages: Spending the time to widen lets the enemy's soft rear harden before the deep drive can reach it
Widening first means driving deep late, so the richest prizes may be defended by the time the exploitation arrives
options.consequence: You make the breakthrough permanent and the exploitation safe, but you drive into a rear that has had time to stiffen. The gap stays open, and the depth you reach is shallower and harder won for the waiting.

costs.resource: every hour spent widening is an hour the soft rear hardens against the deep drive
costs.risk: A penetration secured but exploited late drives into a rear that is no longer soft: the gap is held, but the breakthrough achieves little

options.title: Drive Deep at Once
advantages: Reaches the enemy's rear while it is still soft and unprepared: the richest and cheapest exploitation
Outruns the reseal by being deep in the rear before the reserve can react to the depth at all
disadvantages: Leaves the shoulders thin, so the reserve seals the gap behind the exploitation while it is far away
A deep drive with a closed gap behind it is a force cut off in the enemy's depth, unsupplied and unsupported
options.consequence: You take the soft rear cheaply and deeply, and stake the whole exploitation on the gap not closing behind you. If the reserve seals it, your force is loose in the enemy's depth with no way home.

costs.resource: the shoulders left thin while the whole force drives into the depth
costs.risk: The reserve seals the gap behind the deep drive, and the exploitation is cut off in the enemy rear with the crust closed at its back

options.title: Split — Hold and Drive
advantages: Holds the shoulders with one element while the other exploits: an attempt to keep the gap open and reach the rear at the same time
Hedges against the reseal: if the gap holds, the drive has a road home; if the drive stalls, the held shoulders preserve the penetration
disadvantages: Dividing the exploitation echelon leaves the shoulder-hold too light to stop a concentrated reserve, and the deep drive too light to overrun a hardening rear
A reserve that masses against the thin shoulders breaks them while the deep element is too far away to return
options.consequence: You try to widen and drive at the same time and risk both being too weak. The split keeps the option of a clean exploitation alive, but it invites the reserve to defeat each half in turn.
