Balance it right and the breakthrough both holds and reaches; balance it wrong and it fails on both counts.

costs.resource: the force split between holding the shoulders and driving deep, leaving it lighter at both
costs.risk: A concentrated reserve breaks the thin shoulders while the deep element is too far away to come back: the gap closes and the drive is stranded

entries.event: The exploitation echelon pours through the penetration into the open country beyond the crust. The gap is open and the rear is soft.
{NPC:opfor-commander} commits the mobile reserve toward the shoulders of the gap to begin resealing the penetration.
The reserve reaches the gap's shoulders. The crust begins to weld shut behind the exploitation unless the shoulders are held.
The enemy rear has scraped together blocking forces. The deep prizes are no longer soft and the exploitation meets resistance in the depth.
The penetration is held open and the rear unhinged, or the gap is resealed and the exploitation is cut off in the enemy's depth.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: The penetration must be held open and the rear exploited before the reserve reseals the gap around T+20:00. A gap closed behind the exploitation traps it in the enemy depth. The breakthrough that should have collapsed the line becomes a force to be extracted from behind it instead.

opforSketch.composition: A mobile reserve driving to reseal a penetration. A concentrated force of medium and heavy 'Mechs (50-85 tons) at Veteran quality, fast and undamaged, supported by a mobile armor company (Manticore and Pegasus behavior) built for speed to the gap's shoulders. The defensive crust on the shoulders is the original line's positions, Regular quality, dug in. The enemy rear holds only hastily assembled blocking forces (supply troops and repair-park security) that stiffen over time.
opforSketch.behavior: Counter-penetration doctrine: ignore the deep exploitation and drive the reserve straight for the shoulders of the gap to cut the penetration off at its root. The reserve fights to seal the crust behind the exploitation rather than defend the rear, betting that a cut-off exploitation dies on its own. The shoulder positions hold to pin the widening attempt; the rear blocking forces delay the deep drive without expecting to stop it.

forks.name: OPERATION FLOOD PLAIN
forks.trigger: The penetration was held open and the exploitation drove deep into the rear, unhinging the line; the breakthrough became a collapse.
forks.consequence: The crack has become a flood and {TARGET_FACTION}'s line on {WORLD} is coming apart from behind. The order is to keep the exploitation rolling before the enemy can form a new line in the depth. Your force drives on into the collapsing rear while the defense is still reeling. The water is through the breach; now it runs.

forks.name: OPERATION CUT OFF
forks.trigger: The reserve resealed the gap behind the exploitation; the deep element is cut off in the enemy's depth with the crust closed at its back.
forks.consequence: The gap closed on the wrong side of your force, and the exploitation is loose and unsupplied in the enemy rear. The next operation is to fight that cut-off element back out through the resealed crust before the defender can destroy it in his depth: a breakout in reverse, from the inside out. The breakthrough failed; the line held. The flood is dammed; the force gets clear.

storyElementSeed: A scout lance halts at a crossroads deep behind the broken line, engines idling, looking down an empty road toward an enemy supply park that does not yet know the front has been breached. On the net, the lance leader weighs two things: how far back the rest of the force still is, and how soon the gap might close behind them all.

is-davion.objectives.primary: Pour through the gap and exploit the soft rear before the reserve reseals the crust. Widen the shoulders or drive deep, but turn the breakthrough into a collapse before the gap closes behind you.

is-marik.objectives.primary: Drive the exploitation through the penetration into the enemy rear before the gap closes, choosing where to spend the force between the shoulders and the depth. Command wants the line unhinged, not an echelon stranded behind a resealed crust.

RESERVE_ARRIVAL_HOURS.unit: hours to reserve at the shoulders

inspiration: A contested orbital combat drop onto a defended objective: the assault force scatters across the drop zone on insertion and must rally and concentrate combat power to seize the objective before the defender's mobile reserve rolls up the dispersed sticks one at a time.
skeleton: an orbital combat-drop force lands scattered across a defended drop zone and must rally its dispersed elements into concentrated combat power and seize a fixed objective before the defender's mobile reserve can roll up the isolated sticks piecemeal, where the drop trades the strength of mass for the surprise of arriving anywhere and the whole battle is the race to concentrate before being destroyed in detail on the landing ground
title: OPERATION FALLING STAR
situation: {EMPLOYER} cannot reach the objective in {DISTRICT} on {WORLD} by a ground advance. The enemy holds the approaches in depth, so a march to the objective would mean fighting for every kilometer. The order instead is to land directly on the objective from orbit. The assault force drops in drop cocoons through defended airspace and comes down inside enemy-held territory, behind the front line, on ground the enemy considered secure. The advantage of an orbital drop is reach: the force can arrive anywhere, achieve surprise, and put the objective within immediate striking distance. The cost is concentration. A combat drop does not land in formation. It scatters. {NPC:intel-source} warns that the descent through defended airspace and turbulent air will spread the force across several kilometers of the drop zone. Individual lances, called sticks, will land out of formation and out of radio contact, each one isolated on the ground until it can locate the others. This dispersion estimate is {INTEL_AGE_HOURS} hours old, and a real drop pattern is always looser than the plan. The core problem is simple. The force lands scattered, so it must rally, pulling its separated lances together into one concentrated force, and seize the objective before the enemy's mobile reserve can find the isolated lances and destroy them one at a time. The objective is a fixed installation held by a garrison that does not expect an attack from above. A concentrated force can take it and hold it against the reserve. Concentrating is the hard part. {NPC:opfor-commander} commands the reserve and will do the obvious thing: drive straight for the landing zone and destroy the scattered lances before they can link up, defeating the drop piece by piece while it is still spread out. The terrain is open and broken. It is fast ground for your force to rally across, and just as fast for the reserve to hunt across, with little cover for a lone lance caught before it joins the others. Recommended force: {FORCE_SIZE}. Land, gather the force before the reserve can scatter it permanently, and take the objective. Stay scattered too long and the drop force is destroyed one lance at a time on the ground where it landed.

objectives.primary: Rally the scattered drop force into one concentrated force and seize the fixed objective inside enemy-held territory before the mobile reserve can destroy the separated lances one at a time.
objectives.secondary: Recover and consolidate the isolated lances before the reserve can destroy them. A drop force that takes the objective but loses half its strength to scattered lances will be too weak to hold what it captured.
objectives.bonus: Seize the objective's communications or control center intact during the assault. Capturing the installation in working order, before the garrison can destroy it, is the difference between holding a usable prize and holding a ruin.

complications.name: Scattered on Landing
complications.text: The drop does not land where the plan drew it. The descent through defended airspace and turbulent air spreads the force out, and the lances come down strung across several kilometers of the drop zone, each one alone and out of radio contact until it can move to the others. The first hour on the ground is spent locating your own force, not fighting the enemy.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The drop force starts dispersed across the drop zone instead of concentrated, with its elements outside mutual support and command range. Units must move to rally points to consolidate. Until they are concentrated, isolated lances fight at a severe disadvantage against the massed reserve.

complications.name: Rolled Up in Detail
complications.text: The reserve's entire plan is to reach the scattered lances before they can gather and destroy them one at a time, defeating the drop force while it is still spread out and weak. A lance caught alone by the concentrated reserve is a lost lance. The race to rally is a race to avoid being found first.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The mobile reserve concentrates against isolated lances, engaging your dispersed elements with overwhelming local force. Each lance destroyed before consolidation weakens the rally. The reserve gains a combat bonus against any element still isolated when it makes contact.

complications.name: The Reserve Beats the Rally
complications.text: {NPC:opfor-commander} will not wait for the drop force to organize. He drives his reserve straight for the landing zone the instant the descent is detected, betting that he can reach the scattered force and break it up before it concentrates. Both sides are racing toward the same moment, the moment the drop force is fully assembled: one to reach it, the other to prevent it.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The reserve commits the moment the drop is detected and races for the drop zone. The rally clock and the reserve's arrival clock run against each other. A force that concentrates before the reserve arrives fights it as a massed unit; a force still gathering when the reserve arrives fights it one piece at a time.

complications.name: Open Hunting Ground
complications.text: The drop zone is open and broken. The terrain lets your force rally quickly, but it also lets the reserve hunt just as quickly. A lone lance has little cover to hide in while it moves toward the others, and the same speed that gathers the force also lets the reserve run it down. The terrain helps whoever is concentrated and hurts whoever is alone.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Open terrain speeds up both the rally and the reserve's hunt. Isolated lances get little concealment crossing to rally points. Patches of broken ground offer temporary cover for a lance to consolidate behind, but holding to that cover slows the rally and gives the reserve more time to close in.

decisionPoints.name: Gathering the Force
decisionPoints.context: The force is down and scattered, and the reserve is on its way. You have three options. You can name a single rally point and pull everything to it for maximum strength before moving on the objective. You can drive the nearest lances straight onto the objective to seize it quickly, then rally onto the captured position. Or you can rally in two groups, with one group pinning the reserve while the other concentrates. Each option trades how fast you assemble against how exposed you are while assembling.

options.title: One Rally Point, Full Mass
advantages: Concentrates the entire drop force before committing — the strongest possible attack on the objective and the strongest defense against the reserve
Once the rally is complete, no element has to fight the reserve alone
disadvantages: Pulling every scattered lance to one point takes the most time, and that is time the reserve spends hunting the lances still on the move
Lances far from the rally point must cross the most open ground, exposed, before they join
options.consequence: You assemble the heaviest force and hit the objective hardest, but the slow gather leaves the outlying lances exposed the longest. Reach full strength before the reserve does and you are nearly unstoppable; lose the race and you are strong but missing the lances the reserve picked off along the way.

costs.resource: The time the full rally takes is time the reserve spends hunting the lances still moving to the rally point
costs.risk: Outlying lances caught crossing open ground to the rally point are lost before they join — your full strength minus whatever the reserve destroyed on the way

options.title: Rush the Objective Now
advantages: Drives the nearest lances straight onto the objective before the garrison can prepare or the reserve can arrive — seizes the prize quickly
Rallies the rest of the force onto a captured objective rather than onto open ground
disadvantages: The lances that rush are only a fraction of the force, so they take the objective with little strength against its garrison
A small element on the objective must hold it against both the garrison's counterattack and the reserve while the rest of the force is still gathering
options.consequence: You seize the objective before anyone is set, then stake holding it on the rest of the force reaching the captured position in time. Take it cleanly and the drop force has its anchor; fail and a small element is overrun on the objective alone.

costs.resource: A fraction of the force commits to the objective with little strength, ahead of the main rally
costs.risk: The small seizing element is caught between the garrison and the reserve before the rest of the force can reach the objective to reinforce it

options.title: Rally in Two, Fix and Mass
advantages: One group pins and delays the reserve while the other concentrates undisturbed, buying the rally the time the reserve is trying to deny it
Splits the reserve's attention so it cannot hit the gathering force with its full strength
disadvantages: The pinning group is committed against the reserve before it is concentrated, fighting at a disadvantage to buy time
Dividing the rally means the main group is still missing the pinning group's strength when it moves on the objective
options.consequence: You buy the rally its time by spending one group to hold the reserve's attention, accepting that the pinning group fights hard and early. Done right, the main body assembles cleanly and takes the objective; done wrong, the pinning group is destroyed and the main body is still understrength.

costs.resource: One group spent pinning the reserve before it is concentrated, to buy the other group its rally
costs.risk: The pinning group is overwhelmed before the main body assembles — the reserve breaks it and turns on a rally that is still understrength

entries.event: The drop force comes down scattered across the drop zone. Lances land out of formation and begin moving to rally points as the descent is detected.
{NPC:opfor-commander} commits the mobile reserve toward the landing zone to break up the scattered force before it concentrates.
The reserve reaches the edge of the drop zone and begins hunting isolated lances. The rally must be well advanced or lances will be caught alone.
If rallied, the concentrated force moves on the objective against its garrison. If still scattered, it is being destroyed one lance at a time.
The objective is seized and held by a concentrated force, or the drop force is broken up on the drop zone before it could assemble.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: The drop force must concentrate and seize the objective before the reserve can destroy the scattered lances, by roughly T+18:00. A force still dispersed when the reserve reaches it is destroyed one lance at a time on the landing zone, and the combat drop ends as scattered wreckage inside enemy-held territory.

opforSketch.composition: A garrison plus a mobile reserve inside enemy-held territory. The objective is held by a 'Mech company of mediums (40-60 tons) at Regular quality, dug in around the installation and not expecting an attack from above. The decisive element is a fast mobile reserve of medium and heavy 'Mechs (45-80 tons), Regular-to-Veteran quality, that races to the drop zone, supported by a light armor element (Pegasus and hover behavior) for speed in hunting scattered lances. The reserve's strength is its concentration against a dispersed enemy.
opforSketch.behavior: Counter-drop doctrine: race the mobile reserve to the landing zone and destroy the scattered force one piece at a time before it can concentrate, hitting isolated lances with overwhelming local force. The reserve hunts the dispersed lances and avoids the objective until the drop force is broken up. The objective garrison holds in place against the assault. The reserve fights above all to prevent the rally, on the understanding that a concentrated drop force is a far harder problem than a scattered one.

forks.name: OPERATION PLANTED FLAG
forks.trigger: The drop force concentrated, seized the objective, and held it against the reserve. The deep strike is now an anchor in the enemy's rear.
forks.consequence: An assault force is dug in deep behind {TARGET_FACTION}'s line, on an objective the enemy cannot ignore, and the front is now threatened from behind. The order is to hold the captured objective against the reserve's now-deliberate counterattack until the main effort can link up from the front. Your force holds the ground while the war comes to it. The star came down; now it holds the ground.

forks.name: OPERATION SCATTERED FIELD
forks.trigger: The reserve broke up the drop force before it could concentrate. The force is scattered and being destroyed one lance at a time across the drop zone.
forks.consequence: The drop force failed to gather and is coming apart on the landing zone, its lances cut off and overwhelmed one at a time. The next operation is to recover the surviving scattered elements and get them out of enemy-held territory before they are destroyed piece by piece — a recovery of the broken pieces under a reserve that holds the field. The survivors are brought home. The star fell short; what is left is salvaged.

storyElementSeed: A lone 'Mech comes down hard in a field at dawn, sheds its drop cocoon, and stands alone in open country with no friendly unit in sight. Its pilot calls rally codes into a silent radio channel and turns toward the only smoke on the horizon that might be one of his own.

is-kurita.objectives.primary: Gather the scattered drop force and seize the objective before the enemy reserve can break it up. The Dragon's warriors come down alone and must unite into a single fist before the reserve finds them apart.

is-davion.objectives.primary: Rally the scattered lances into a concentrated force and take the objective before the mobile reserve can destroy them one at a time. Come down, gather fast, and hit hard — a drop force destroyed piece by piece is a drop force wasted.

DROP_DISPERSAL_KM.unit: km of scatter across the drop zone

inspiration: The reduction of a hardened, partly-automated planetary-defence fortress complex: a web of mutually-supporting works defended by tireless caretaker drones with no morale, where the human lever is the control node and the choice is to dark the drones at the node or fight every gun in the complex.
skeleton: an assault force must reduce a fortress complex of mutually-supporting hardened works defended by automated, morale-less caretaker units that never tire and fight to destruction, where the human-held control node can be taken to dark the whole automated net at once but sits at the complex's hardest center, so the crux is whether to drive for the node through the heaviest ground to switch the drones off or grind down a self-defending fortress emplacement by emplacement
title: OPERATION SILENT KEEPER
situation: {TARGET_FACTION} holds {DISTRICT} on {WORLD} behind an old Star League fortress the enemy now uses. It is a planetary-defense complex of hardened works, gun bastions, and automated defenses. This kind of lostech installation takes a regiment to build and a war to break. {EMPLOYER} needs it reduced. That is unlike breaking any line of trenches, because most of the fortress has no human crew. It is run by caretaker units: automated defense drones. These lostech machines work the bastions and the kill-zones on their own. They do not tire, flinch, or break. They will fight until destroyed, patient because they feel nothing. {NPC:intel-source} maps a complex of mutually supporting works. Each bastion is covered by the guns of the next. The automated network ties the whole thing into one defense. Reducing it one bastion at a time means grinding through each murderous position in turn. The survey is {INTEL_AGE_DAYS} days old, but the complex has not changed. Automated works do not need to. There is one weak point. A control node at the center runs the whole automated network. It is a hardened command post, and it is the one place where humans control the defense. Take the node and every drone shuts down at once. The fortress dies in a single stroke. The catch is where the node sits. It is at the deepest, most heavily covered point of the complex, ringed by the very guns it controls. To reach it, you must fight through the worst of the fortress to shut down the rest. So you have two ways to reduce it. Drive for the node through the heaviest defenses, shut down the network, and walk into a dead fortress. Or grind the complex down one gun at a time, the long and bloody way, taking each bastion under the fire of the next. {NPC:opfor-commander} commands the human garrison and will fight hardest to hold the node. It is the difference between a working fortress and a field of scrap. The terrain is the complex itself: hardened, overlooked, every approach covered by something that never sleeps. Recommended force: {FORCE_SIZE}. Shut down the control node or grind down the fortress. Either one reduces it, and they cost in opposite ways.

objectives.primary: Reduce the planetary-defense fortress complex and take it. Either seize the control node to shut down the automated network in one stroke, or grind down the hardened works one bastion at a time.
objectives.secondary: Take the control node and its automated network intact rather than wrecking them. A fortress reduced with its defenses captured in working order becomes {EMPLOYER}'s own shield on {WORLD}; one fought to rubble is just a ruin and a salvage yard.
objectives.bonus: Capture the complex's lostech defense systems and their control software intact. The automated-defense technology itself is worth more to {EMPLOYER} than the ground it stands on.

complications.name: The Tireless Drones
complications.text: The caretaker units that operate the fortress are not soldiers and cannot be made to act like them. They do not tire, do not lose their nerve, and do not break under pressure or fall back to save themselves. They fight from their bastions to destruction, as steady in the first hour as in the last. There is no morale to crack and no commander to outthink — only machines to be destroyed or switched off.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Automated defenses never check morale, never break contact, and fight at full effectiveness until destroyed. Tactics that would rout a human garrison achieve nothing against them. Each drone bastion must be physically destroyed or else shut down via the control node. The drones do not pursue or maneuver; they hold position and fire from their works.

complications.name: Mutually-Supporting Works
complications.text: The bastions are positioned to cover each other. No single work can be assaulted without coming under the guns of the next, and the automated network concentrates the fire of the whole complex on anything that threatens any part of it. Reducing the fortress one emplacement at a time means taking each one in the crossfire of the others.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Each bastion is covered by the fire of the adjacent works. Assaulting one draws supporting fire from the others, and the automated network coordinates that fire without delay. Reducing the fortress one emplacement at a time takes attrition from the supporting works at each step, until enough of the network is destroyed to break the mutual support.

complications.name: The Keeper at the Center
complications.text: The control node is the weak point, and it sits where the fortress is strongest: the deepest, most heavily covered point of the complex, ringed by the guns it commands. To reach it is to fight through the heaviest defenses in the fortress. Taking the node shuts down everything at once, but the route to it runs beneath all of it.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Seizing the control node immediately disables all automated defenses across the complex. But the node is at the complex's hardened center, surrounded by the densest mutual support. The drive to it is the costliest single approach in the fortress, fought under the concentrated fire of the network until the node falls and the network shuts down.

complications.name: The Last Wipe
complications.text: The human garrison knows the node is everything. If it is about to fall, they may erase the control system rather than surrender it intact — shutting down the drones, yes, but destroying the lostech network and the technology along with it, denying {EMPLOYER} the prize even as they lose the fortress.
complications.mechanicalEffect: If the control node is taken by direct assault without first cutting the garrison's command link, roll for the wipe. On a wipe, the automated network shuts down (the fortress is reduced) but the control system and its lostech are destroyed, voiding the secondary and bonus objectives. Cutting the command link before the final assault removes the roll.

decisionPoints.name: Keeper or Fortress
decisionPoints.context: The complex can be reduced two ways, and they cost in opposite ways. Drive for the control node through the fortress's hardened center and switch the whole network off at once — fast and decisive, but through the worst defenses in the place. Or grind the bastions down one at a time the long way — sure and methodical, but paid for in attrition under crossfire. Or split the effort, pinning the outer works while a spearhead drives for the node, and risk both efforts being too weak for what they meet.

options.title: Drive for the Control Node
advantages: Shuts down the entire automated network in a single stroke — the whole fortress goes silent the moment the node falls
Avoids grinding through every bastion; one decisive thrust ends the defense
disadvantages: The node sits at the hardened center under the concentrated fire of the whole network — the costliest approach in the complex
A thrust that stalls short of the node leaves a force pinned at the fortress's deepest point with every gun still active
options.consequence: You bet everything on reaching the control node through the worst of the fortress. Take the node and the whole defense shuts down at once; stall short and the spearhead is caught at the center under fire from a network still fully active.

costs.resource: The spearhead's strength spent driving through the fortress's hardened center under the concentrated automated fire
costs.risk: A drive that stalls short of the node leaves the force pinned at the complex's deepest point with every drone still firing

options.title: Grind the Bastions Down
advantages: Reduces the fortress methodically, breaking the mutual support one work at a time until the network comes apart
No single catastrophic thrust — each bastion taken reduces the fire on the next
disadvantages: Each emplacement is taken under the crossfire of the others — slow, and paid for in steady attrition
The long grind gives the human garrison time to prepare the node and wears down the assault before it reaches the center
options.consequence: You take the fortress the sure way and pay for it the long way, taking losses at each bastion under the guns of the rest. The complex falls for certain, but the force that takes it is worn down one emplacement at a time.

costs.resource: Steady attrition reducing each bastion under the supporting fire of the others
costs.risk: The long grind wears the assault down before it reaches the center — the fortress falls, but to a force too depleted to hold or exploit it

options.title: Fix the Works, Spear the Node
advantages: Pins the outer bastions with one element while a spearhead drives for the node, keeping the network's fire divided off the thrust
Hedges between the two methods: if the spearhead reaches the node the network shuts down, and if it stalls the pinning force is already reducing the works
disadvantages: Dividing the assault leaves the pinning force too weak to reduce the works quickly and the spearhead too weak to be sure of the node
The automated network does not tire — a pinning force holding the outer works is under unrelenting fire with no respite to exploit
options.consequence: You try to shut down the control node and grind down the fortress at the same time, dividing the network's fire at the cost of strength at both points. Balanced right, the spearhead reaches a node whose covering fire has been drawn away; balanced wrong, both efforts stall under guns that never let up.

costs.resource: The assault split between pinning the outer works and spearheading the node, weaker at both
costs.risk: The tireless network holds both the pinning force and the spearhead under unrelenting fire — divided strength stalls at both the works and the center

entries.event: The assault enters the complex. The automated network detects it and the whole fortress opens fire with the steadiness of machines that do not startle.
The mutually supporting works concentrate the network's fire on the assault's main effort. The human garrison takes its positions at the control node.
The main effort reaches the inner works — either the drive for the node enters the hardened center, or the grind has broken the first ring of bastions.
The fight for the control node, or for the last mutually supporting bastions. If the node is about to fall, the garrison considers the wipe.
The network shuts down, by the node taken or the last bastion destroyed. Or the assault is fought to a standstill under guns that never tired.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: The automated network must be shut down by roughly T+24:00, by seizing the control node or destroying the last mutually supporting bastion. A fortress still fully active by then has worn the assault down under fire that never slackens. The reduction becomes a withdrawal from a fortress that does not feel the losses it inflicts.

opforSketch.composition: A hardened fortress complex, mostly automated. The bastions are held by automated caretaker defense units — lostech turret and emplacement drones (treat as fixed and semi-mobile combatants, 30-70 tons-equivalent firepower) at uniformly high effectiveness, mutually supporting, that never check morale and fight to destruction. The human garrison is a small 'Mech element of mediums and heavies (50-80 tons), Veteran quality, concentrated at the control node, plus combat engineers operating the node's systems. Fixed fortification throughout.
opforSketch.behavior: Automated fortress doctrine: the caretaker drones hold their bastions and pour mutually supporting fire onto any threat without fatigue, hesitation, or withdrawal, fighting to their own destruction from prepared works. They do not maneuver or pursue. The human garrison defends the control node to the last to keep the network running, and will erase the control system rather than surrender it intact. The machines fight the battle; the people guard the switch that runs them.

forks.name: OPERATION OWNED WALLS
forks.trigger: The fortress was reduced and the control node and its network taken substantially intact. The lostech defenses are now {EMPLOYER}'s.
forks.consequence: The fortress that held {WORLD}'s interior is taken whole, its automated network captured in working order and turned outward in {EMPLOYER}'s name. The order is to hold the captured complex and bring its defenses back online against {TARGET_FACTION}'s inevitable attempt to retake or destroy it. Your force garrisons the fortress it just captured. The walls are taken; now they are held, and made to answer to a new hand.

forks.name: OPERATION COLD BASTION
forks.trigger: The assault was fought to a standstill in the complex, or worn down under the tireless network before the node or the last bastion fell.
forks.consequence: The fortress held and the assault is spent against works that never tired. The next operation is to disengage the worn-down force from the complex and pull it clear before the garrison can sortie against an exhausted attacker — a withdrawal from a fortress that takes no notice of what it cost you. The complex is reduced another day, the harder way. The walls held; the force gets clear.

storyElementSeed: A gun bastion keeps firing in a steady, unhurried rhythm long after the works around it have gone quiet. There is no crew inside it and no voice on any channel from it, just the same measured shots arriving on time. Someone finally destroys it. The silence afterward feels different from the silence of a dead man's gun.

is-davion.objectives.primary: Reduce the fortress complex and take the works — drive for the control node to shut down the automated network in a single stroke, or grind the bastions down under their own crossfire. Switch off the control node or destroy every gun; both win, at opposite cost.

is-steiner.objectives.primary: Reduce the planetary-defense complex by seizing the control node or grinding down the works, and take it intact if you can. The lostech network is worth more than the ground it sits on — shut down the control node without erasing it, and the fortress becomes an asset on the books, not a salvage line.

NODE_DEPTH_KM.unit: km to the control node through the complex

inspiration: The deliberate assault on a fortified mountain massif: a wall of mutually-supporting peak strongpoints under observed fire from the heights, where grinding every peak bleeds the assault white and the real problem is finding and taking the one dominating feature that makes the rest of the massif untenable.
skeleton: an assault force must break a fortified mountain massif of mutually-supporting peak strongpoints overlooked by enemy observation from the heights, where assaulting each peak in turn under plunging fire bleeds the force white, but one dominating feature commands the whole massif so taking it makes the other strongpoints untenable, and the crux is reading which height is the keystone and forcing it up covered ground before the assault is ground down peak by peak
title: OPERATION HIGH GROUND
situation: The road through {DISTRICT} on {WORLD} runs beneath a mountain wall, and {TARGET_FACTION} has turned that wall into a fortress that watches everything. The massif is a chain of fortified peaks. Each one is a strongpoint of dug-in positions and hardened guns, placed to cover the others. All of it overlooks the only ground an army can move through to reach the interior. As long as the enemy holds the heights, he sees every meter of the approaches and drops fire on them from above. Nothing passes beneath the massif while it is in his hands. {EMPLOYER} has to take it, and the obvious method is the wrong one. Assaulting the peaks one after another, under plunging fire from all the rest, bleeds the assault white. It spends a battalion on a chain of summits that each cost more than they are worth. {NPC:intel-source} has the massif mapped, and the map shows the key: the peaks are not equal. One feature dominates the chain. Its guns and observation tie the whole massif together. Take it and the rest of the strongpoints cannot hold, because they are now overlooked from above and their mutual support is broken. The survey is {INTEL_AGE_DAYS} days old, and the heights have only been dug deeper since. So one question decides the operation. Which height is the keystone, and can it be taken before the assault is ground down on peaks that do not matter? Take the dominating feature and the massif unravels. Read it wrong, and send the assault up a peak that is not the keystone, and you spend the force on a summit that changes nothing while the real keystone watches you do it. The catch is that the keystone is the hardest to reach and the best defended. Every step of the approach is overlooked from the very height you are trying to take. {NPC:opfor-commander} commands the massif and knows which peak is the keystone better than you do. He holds it most strongly and hopes you exhaust yourself on the others first. Recommended force: {FORCE_SIZE}. Read the high ground, force the keystone up covered slopes, and the wall comes down. Take the wrong peak and the mountain bleeds you for nothing.

objectives.primary: Take the dominating feature that commands the fortified massif. Breaking it breaks the mutual support of the peak strongpoints and makes the chain untenable, so the road beneath the heights opens.
objectives.secondary: Avoid grinding the force down on the lesser peaks before reaching the keystone. An assault that spends its strength on summits that do not command the chain will reach the dominating feature too weak to take it.
objectives.bonus: Take the massif's observation and fire-direction post on the keystone intact — the eyes that command the approaches, turned to watch {TARGET_FACTION}'s own routes once the height is {EMPLOYER}'s.

complications.name: Plunging Fire
complications.text: Everything below the peaks is overlooked. The enemy on the heights sees the assault forming up and climbing, and drops fire on it from above, where his guns have the advantage of height and his observers have the whole approach laid out in front of them. An assault up these slopes climbs into fire that falls on it the entire way, with little cover on the bare upper ground.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The approaches to the peaks, and the assaults up them, are under plunging fire from the heights still in enemy hands. Attacking units take a height-disadvantage penalty and have reduced cover on the upper slopes. Taking the dominating feature removes the plunging fire from the peaks it overlooks; until then, every climb is made under observed fire from above.

complications.name: The Keystone Is Hidden in Plain Sight
complications.text: Which peak is the keystone is not obvious from below. Several heights look dominant; only one truly commands the chain, and choosing the wrong one is the easiest and costliest mistake on the massif. The enemy holds them all and gives no sign of which one he most fears to lose.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The dominating feature must be correctly identified before the main assault commits. Committing against a lesser peak spends the assault on a summit that does not break the chain's mutual support. Intelligence work and reconnaissance reduce the risk of misidentifying the keystone, but the enemy garrisons all the peaks to disguise which one it is.

complications.name: Ground Down Peak by Peak
complications.text: The temptation, and the trap, is to take the massif the methodical way: one peak, then the next, then the next. Do that and you are a spent force by the time you reach the one that matters. Each lesser summit assaulted under fire from the others costs strength the assault needs for the keystone, and the chain is built to make you pay for every height.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Force spent assaulting non-keystone peaks is attrition the assault carries forward. Reaching the dominating feature after grinding through the lesser peaks means assaulting the hardest height with a depleted force. The cheapest way to reduce the massif is to take the keystone before the chain can extract its toll on the lesser summits.

complications.name: Covered Approach to the Crest
complications.text: The dominating feature is reached up ground where every step is overlooked from the crest itself. There is one covered approach, a route through the dead ground of a ridge or a steep gully that climbs out of the worst of the observation. But it is narrow and slow, and it is the obvious covered line, which means the defender has thought about it too.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The direct approach to the keystone is fully overlooked from its crest. A single covered route exists in the terrain's dead ground, but it is narrow (restricting frontage) and may be watched. Using the covered approach reduces fire on the climb at the cost of speed and the risk of a prepared ambush on the route.

decisionPoints.name: Forcing the Keystone
decisionPoints.context: The dominating feature has been identified and the assault must reach it. You have three options. Climb the covered route through the dead ground — slow, narrow, out of the worst fire, but the line the defender may have watched. Storm straight up the overlooked face — fast and bloody, into plunging fire the whole way. Or take a flanking lesser peak first to suppress the keystone's supporting fire, spending strength on the way in order to spare it on the crest. Each option pays for the height in a different currency.

options.title: Climb the Covered Route
advantages: Approaches the keystone through the dead ground, out of the worst of the plunging fire, so the assault reaches the crest with its strength intact
Arrives where the defender's observation is weakest and the climb is least visible
disadvantages: The covered route is narrow and slow, restricting the assault to a thin frontage and a long climb
It is the obvious covered line — the defender may have it watched and prepared as an ambush where the ground forces the assault into single file
options.consequence: If the route is clear, you reach the crest with the force unspent, but you climb slow and thin up a line the defender may have anticipated. Either you achieve surprise in the dead ground, or you walk into a prepared ambush where you cannot deploy.

costs.resource: The assault climbs slow and thin up the narrow covered route to spare itself the plunging fire
costs.risk: A covered route the defender watched becomes an ambush where the ground forces the assault into single file — strength saved from the fire, then spent in the trap

options.title: Storm the Overlooked Face
advantages: The most direct line to the crest — the fastest way onto the dominating feature before the defender can shift strength to it
A broad-front assault puts the maximum weight on the keystone at once
disadvantages: The face is overlooked from the crest the whole way — the assault climbs into plunging fire from start to summit
An assault that stalls on the open face leaves a force pinned on bare ground under fire from directly above
options.consequence: You take the keystone the fast, direct, costly way, climbing into fire the entire height. Take it quickly and the chain unravels; stall on the face and the assault is broken on the slope under guns it cannot reach.

costs.resource: The assault's strength spent climbing the overlooked face into plunging fire to reach the crest quickly
costs.risk: An assault stalled on the open face is pinned on bare ground under fire from the crest above — the keystone holds and the assault dies on its slope

options.title: Take a Flanking Peak First
advantages: Seizing an adjacent height first suppresses the keystone's supporting fire and overlooks part of its approach in turn
Removes the keystone's mutual support before the main assault climbs it
disadvantages: Spends strength and time on a lesser peak before the one that matters — risking the very grinding-down the operation is meant to avoid
The flanking peak is itself defended and covered; taking it is a battle before the main battle
options.consequence: You reduce the keystone's defenses by taking its neighbor first, accepting that you spend some of the assault to do it. Done right, the dominating feature falls to a force that has broken its support; done wrong, you have ground yourself down on the flank before reaching the height that counts.

costs.resource: Strength and time spent taking a flanking peak to suppress the keystone's supporting fire
costs.risk: The flank costs more than it saves — the assault grinds itself down on the lesser peak and reaches the keystone too weak to take it

entries.event: The assault moves against the massif. The peak strongpoints open plunging fire on the approaches from the heights.
The main effort commits toward the identified keystone. The other peaks pour supporting fire onto the climb.
The assault reaches the slopes of the dominating feature. {NPC:opfor-commander} shifts what reserve he has to hold the keystone he knows is decisive.
The fight for the crest of the dominating feature. If it falls, the lesser peaks come under its observation and their mutual support breaks.
The keystone is taken and the chain unravels, or the assault is ground down on the heights with the massif still commanding the road.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: The dominating feature must be taken by roughly T+24:00, before the assault is ground down on the heights. A massif still in enemy hands by then still commands the road beneath it. The assault becomes a withdrawal off slopes that overlooked every step of it.

opforSketch.composition: A fortified mountain defense: a reinforced 'Mech battalion-equivalent of mediums and heavies (45-80 tons) at Regular-to-Veteran quality dug into the peak strongpoints, heavily reinforced by hardened fixed guns and fortifications on the heights and observation posts commanding the approaches. Minimal armor, because the broken high ground is nearly impassable to vehicles off the few mountain tracks. The keystone is held most strongly, with the best of the garrison and a small mobile reserve to reinforce it.
opforSketch.behavior: Mountain-fortress doctrine: hold the peaks as mutually supporting strongpoints, drop plunging fire on every approach, and make the assault pay for each height under the guns of the others. The garrison holds the dominating feature most strongly and hopes the assault exhausts itself on the lesser peaks first. Fixed positions fight in place to destruction; the small reserve shifts only to hold the keystone, the one height whose loss unravels the whole defense.

forks.name: OPERATION OPEN PASS
forks.trigger: The dominating feature was taken, the chain's mutual support broken, and the lesser peaks rendered untenable. The road beneath the massif is open.
forks.consequence: The mountain wall is broken from its commanding height, and the road into {DISTRICT}'s interior lies open beneath it. The order is to push the advance through the opened ground before the enemy can fall back to a new line. Your force drives down off the heights and through the pass the massif used to seal. The high ground is taken; the road is free.

forks.name: OPERATION BLED WHITE
forks.trigger: The assault was ground down on the heights — the keystone misidentified or never taken — and the massif still commands the road.
forks.consequence: The mountain held and the assault is spent on its slopes, the dominating feature still in enemy hands and the road beneath it still closed. The next operation is to hold the captured ground low on the massif and recover the assault's strength before the garrison counterattacks downhill against an exhausted force. The wall stands; it will be forced again later, using what this attempt learned about which height is the keystone. The mountain bled the assault; the force holds and takes stock.

storyElementSeed: A recon officer lies among the rocks below the massif at first light, studying the peaks one by one through binoculars. From the way the guns are laid and the tracks are worn, he tries to read which summit the enemy would die to hold. The whole assault will go where he points, and the mountain gives nothing away for free.

is-kurita.objectives.primary: Take the dominating height that commands the massif and the chain of strongpoints falls with it. Identify the keystone, force it up covered ground, and open the road. The Dragon does not bleed a battalion on summits that do not matter.

is-marik.objectives.primary: Seize the height that commands the fortified massif, breaking the mutual support of the peaks, so the road beneath opens. Identify the keystone before you commit — command will not pay for a chain of summits taken the wrong way around.

inspiration: The destruction of a hostile lodgment: a deliberate concentric assault to collapse an enemy bridgehead with its back to a water or obstacle line before its build-up reaches breakout weight, racing the enemy's reinforcement clock with the choice of hitting it early-and-thin or late-and-prepared.
skeleton: an attacking force must collapse a hostile lodgment pinned against a water or obstacle line by concentric assault before its build-up reaches breakout strength, racing the enemy's reinforcement clock where striking early hits a thin but unprepared lodgment and striking late hits a strong dug-in one, so the crux is timing the assault against the enemy's reinforcement and driving the bridgehead back into the obstacle at its back before it can break out
title: OPERATION DRIVEN PILE
situation: {TARGET_FACTION} has gotten a force across the obstacle line in {DISTRICT} on {WORLD} and is trying to turn a toehold into a breakout. The enemy holds a lodgment with its back to the water. It is a bridgehead on your side of the river barrier, fed across a crossing he has built, building up strength on ground he should not hold. Right now it is contained: a perimeter pinned against the water, not yet strong enough to break out and drive into the interior beyond. {EMPLOYER} means to destroy it before it can. The plan is to collapse the lodgment by attacking it from all sides at once and drive it back into the obstacle behind it, before the build-up reaches breakout strength. The whole operation is a race against the enemy's reinforcement clock. {NPC:intel-source} reports the lodgment steadily feeding fresh strength across the crossing. Every hour it grows stronger, deeper, and more dug in. This report is {INTEL_AGE_HOURS} hours old, and the flow across the crossing has not slowed. That sets the timing problem. Strike early and you hit a thin, unprepared lodgment, but you go in before your own force is fully massed, with less strength than a deliberate assault. Strike late and you bring your full strength, but you hit a lodgment that used the time to dig in and thicken. Either way the goal is the same: collapse the perimeter and drive it into the water before it can break out. {NPC:opfor-commander} commands the lodgment and is racing the other way. He is building strength to break out before you can collapse him, ready to turn defense into breakout the moment he has the weight. The terrain is the near bank of the obstacle: low, wet ground the lodgment is pinned against. The enemy's crossing is its one lifeline, the one thing it cannot survive without. Recommended force: {FORCE_SIZE}. Time the assault against his build-up, collapse the perimeter, and drive the bridgehead back into the obstacle. Hit too early and you are too weak. Hit too late and he breaks out before you can close in.

objectives.primary: Collapse the enemy lodgment by attacking from all sides at once and drive it back into the obstacle behind it before the build-up reaches breakout strength. Destroy or capture the bridgehead force.
objectives.secondary: Cut or hold the enemy's crossing over the obstacle during the assault. A lodgment cut off from its crossing cannot be reinforced or withdrawn, and collapses far faster than one still fed across the water.
objectives.bonus: Take the crossing itself intact — the bridge or ford the enemy built over the obstacle, turned to {EMPLOYER}'s own use for the counterattack onto the far bank once the lodgment is gone.

complications.name: The Reinforcement Clock
complications.text: The lodgment grows by the hour. Fresh strength crosses the obstacle into the bridgehead steadily, thickening the perimeter and deepening the dug-in positions. The assault races that growth: every hour of delay means a stronger lodgment to collapse, until the moment it is strong enough to break out instead of defend.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Track a lodgment build-up clock. The bridgehead's strength and preparation increase each interval as reinforcements cross. Past a threshold the lodgment reaches breakout strength and shifts from defending to attacking outward, sharply raising the FAILURE fork's threat. Cutting the crossing halts the build-up.

complications.name: Early and Thin, or Late and Strong
complications.text: There is no good time to attack, only two bad ones. Strike before your force is fully concentrated and you hit a weak lodgment with a weak hand. Wait until your full strength is massed and you hit a strong lodgment that used the same hours to dig in. The assault's timing is a bet on which trade is cheaper, made against a clock that only runs one way.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The assault's start time trades the attacker's concentration against the defender's preparation. An early assault commits before full force is massed but against a thin perimeter; a late assault brings full strength but against a dug-in perimeter. The reinforcement clock makes waiting progressively worse.

complications.name: Back to the Water
complications.text: The lodgment is pinned against the obstacle, and that is the advantage to exploit. A perimeter driven inward has nowhere to retreat but into the water behind it. Collapse it inward and the bridgehead is destroyed against its own barrier. But the same water means a cornered enemy fights with the desperation of a force that cannot run.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The lodgment's back is against the obstacle. A collapsed perimeter cannot withdraw and is destroyed or captured. But the bridgehead force, unable to retreat, fights without the option of breaking contact, defending each position harder than a force with a line of retreat would.

complications.name: Ready to Break Out
complications.text: {NPC:opfor-commander} is not only defending. The moment he has the strength, he turns the lodgment from a bridgehead into a breakout, driving outward to expand the foothold into the interior before the assault can close in. A lodgment left too long does not wait to be collapsed; it attacks first.
complications.mechanicalEffect: If the build-up clock reaches breakout strength before the assault collapses the lodgment, the bridgehead force attacks outward to break out of the perimeter. The attacker, expecting to assault a defender, is met by a breakout instead — a head-on collision on the enemy's terms, routing toward the FAILURE fork.

decisionPoints.name: Timing the Assault
decisionPoints.context: The lodgment grows while your force gathers, and the two clocks cross at some hour you must pick. You have three options. Strike early with what you have against a thin perimeter. Wait for full strength and hit a dug-in perimeter. Or cut the crossing first to freeze the build-up, then collapse a starved lodgment at your leisure. Each option times the attack differently against the enemy's reinforcement.

options.title: Strike Early and Thin
advantages: Hits the lodgment before it can dig in or thicken — a weak, unprepared perimeter to collapse
Beats the build-up to the punch, well before any breakout strength is reached
disadvantages: Goes in before your own force is fully concentrated — a weak assault, with less strength than a deliberate one
An early assault that stalls against even a thin perimeter gives the lodgment time to reinforce mid-battle
options.consequence: You hit the lodgment at its weakest, but with a hand that is also weak. Carry the thin perimeter quickly and the bridgehead collapses before it could grow; stall and you are a weak force against a lodgment reinforcing as you fight.

costs.resource: The assault commits before the attacking force is fully concentrated, trading strength for the enemy's weakness
costs.risk: An early assault that stalls fights a lodgment reinforcing mid-battle — too weak for a perimeter growing stronger by the hour

options.title: Mass Full Weight First
advantages: Brings the attacker's full concentrated strength against the lodgment — the heaviest possible attack
A massed assault from all sides can collapse even a prepared perimeter in one decisive stroke
disadvantages: The hours spent massing are hours the lodgment spends digging in and thickening — a strong, prepared perimeter to break
Wait too long and the build-up reaches breakout strength, and the assault meets a breakout instead of a defense
options.consequence: You hit the lodgment with everything, against a perimeter the same delay made strong. Mass and strike before breakout strength and the heavy attack collapses it; wait a beat too long and he breaks out into your concentration first.

costs.resource: The hours spent massing full strength are hours the lodgment digs in and approaches breakout strength
costs.risk: A late assault meets a lodgment at breakout strength — the defender attacks outward first and the assault becomes a head-on collision on his terms

options.title: Cut the Crossing First
advantages: Cutting the crossing freezes the build-up — the lodgment can no longer be reinforced and begins to wither
Turns off the race: a starved lodgment can be collapsed deliberately, at full strength, on your timetable
disadvantages: Reaching and cutting the crossing means committing force to the edge of the obstacle, under the lodgment's fire, before the main assault
The crossing is the one thing the lodgment will defend hardest — cutting it is a battle in itself, and a failed attempt warns the enemy and wastes the effort
options.consequence: You take away the enemy's clock by cutting his lifeline to the far bank, accepting that reaching the crossing is its own hard fight. Cut it and the lodgment is yours to collapse at leisure; fail and you have spent strength and tipped your hand with the build-up still running.

costs.resource: Force committed to reaching and cutting the crossing under the lodgment's fire before the main collapse
costs.risk: A failed cut wastes the effort against the enemy's best-defended point and warns him, with the build-up clock still running

entries.event: The assault opens against the lodgment's perimeter. The bridgehead force holds its positions with the water at its back and reinforcements still crossing.
The assault presses the perimeter inward from all sides. {NPC:opfor-commander} feeds fresh strength across the crossing to thicken the threatened sectors.
If not yet collapsed, the lodgment nears breakout strength. The status of the crossing decides whether the build-up continues or the bridgehead starts to wither.
The decisive phase: the perimeter is driven back toward the water, or the lodgment reaches breakout strength and attacks outward.
The lodgment is collapsed into the obstacle, or it has broken out of the perimeter into the interior beyond.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: The lodgment must be collapsed and driven back into the obstacle before it reaches breakout strength, by roughly T+20:00. A bridgehead that reaches breakout strength first attacks outward into the interior. The operation to destroy a contained lodgment becomes a battle to contain a breakout that is already loose.

opforSketch.composition: A lodgment building toward breakout: a 'Mech force of mediums and heavies (45-85 tons) at Regular-to-Veteran quality holding a perimeter pinned against the obstacle, thickening hour by hour as reinforcements cross, supported by an armor element (Manticore and SRM-carrier behavior) and dug-in positions that deepen over time. The crossing over the obstacle is held hardest of all. Strength and preparation increase on the build-up clock until breakout strength is reached.
opforSketch.behavior: Bridgehead doctrine: hold and expand the lodgment, dig in and thicken the perimeter while feeding strength across the crossing, and turn to break out into the interior the moment breakout strength is reached. With its back to the water the force cannot withdraw and defends each position to the last. The crossing is defended above all as the lodgment's lifeline. Once at breakout strength it shifts decisively from defense to a drive outward.

forks.name: OPERATION CLEARED BANK
forks.trigger: The lodgment was collapsed and driven into the obstacle before reaching breakout strength. The bridgehead is destroyed or taken, and the near bank is cleared.
forks.consequence: The enemy's foothold on your side of the obstacle is gone, and the crossing he built over it is in your hands or under your guns. The order is to push across the obstacle onto the far bank while the enemy is reeling from losing his bridgehead. Your force turns the captured crossing into a crossing of your own. The bridgehead is driven into the water; now the bank is yours.

forks.name: OPERATION OVER THE TOP
forks.trigger: The lodgment reached breakout strength and attacked outward, or the assault failed to collapse it in time. The bridgehead has broken out into the interior.
forks.consequence: The lodgment is loose. It broke out of the perimeter before the assault could close in, and an enemy force is now driving into the interior beyond the obstacle. The next operation is to contain and pin the breakout before it can reach its objectives deeper in, a fighting defense to stop what should have been destroyed against the water. The bridgehead held; the breakout runs. The assault turns into a containment.

storyElementSeed: A company commander watches the enemy bridgehead through the morning haze and listens to the steady traffic of reinforcements crossing the river into it. On the radio he weighs it out loud. Every hour of waiting brings up more of his own strength, and just as surely more of the enemy's. He does not like either side of it.

is-davion.objectives.primary: Collapse the enemy lodgment and drive it back into the water before it can break out. Time the assault against his build-up, cut his crossing if you can, and drive the bridgehead into the obstacle behind it.

is-steiner.objectives.primary: Destroy the enemy bridgehead by attacking from all sides at once before its build-up reaches breakout strength, cutting its crossing to freeze the reinforcement. Command wants the near bank cleared and the crossing taken. Collapse the lodgment; do not let it grow into a breakout.

inspiration: The deliberate breaching of a deep prepared obstacle belt: cut and hold clear lanes through minefields, anti-'Mech ditches and wire under fire so the heavy weight can pass, where the lanes are everything and the defender's plan is to re-close them and trap whatever has gone through.
skeleton: an assault force must cut and hold open clear lanes through a deep prepared belt of minefields, anti-'Mech ditches and obstacles under fire so the heavy weight can pass, where the breach is made by engineers not by maneuver and lane integrity rather than ground is the decisive thing, and the defender's plan is to close the lanes behind the units that pass and trap them in the belt, so the crux is keeping the gaps open against an enemy fighting to re-seal them
title: OPERATION CLEAR LANE
situation: {TARGET_FACTION} could not hold the open ground in {DISTRICT} on {WORLD} with troops, so he filled it with obstacles instead. The approach to the interior runs through a deep prepared belt: minefields kilometers across, anti-'Mech ditches cut deep enough to trap a war machine to the waist, dragon's-teeth, and wire. Guns cover all of it, positioned to fire into the obstacles rather than over them. It cannot be charged. A 'Mech that drives in blind bogs down in a ditch or loses a leg to a mine and dies where it stops, under fire it cannot answer. The belt has to be breached, and breaching is engineer work, not maneuver. {EMPLOYER}'s plan is a deliberate breach. Under covering fire, combat engineers cut clear lanes through the belt: safe paths through the mines, ramps over the ditches, gaps blown in the wire. The heavy units file through those marked lanes to reach the open ground beyond. The lanes are the entire operation. Not the ground, not the strongpoints, the lanes. {NPC:intel-source} maps the belt's depth and the guns covering it. That survey is {INTEL_AGE_DAYS} days old, and the enemy has only thickened the belt since. It also warns of the defender's real plan. He does not mean to stop the breach at the wire. He means to let part of the force through, then close the lanes behind it: re-mine the cleared paths, drop fresh fire on the gaps, and seal the belt with friendly units stranded on the far side, trapped between a re-closed obstacle field and the defense beyond. A lane cut is not a lane held. The whole fight is keeping the gaps open against an enemy working to re-seal them, while the heavy units file through a few narrow paths that everything in the belt is trying to close. {NPC:opfor-commander} commands the defense and will fight the lanes, not the assault. He counterattacks the breach sites, harasses the gaps with fire, and times his re-seal to trap the most force on the wrong side of it. The terrain is the belt itself: open ground turned into a deep trap where movement is confined to whatever paths the engineers can cut and hold. Recommended force: {FORCE_SIZE}. Cut the lanes, hold them open, and pass the heavy units through. Let the enemy close them behind you, and the force that got through is sealed inside the belt with the obstacle at its back.

objectives.primary: Cut clear lanes through the deep obstacle belt under fire and keep them open against the defender's re-seal. Pass the heavy units through to the open ground beyond the belt.
objectives.secondary: Hold the breach sites and the lane mouths against the counterattack throughout the passage. Lanes cut but lost while the force is still filing through will strand whatever is caught in the belt.
objectives.bonus: Take the belt's obstacle-control and fire-direction post intact — the positions that cover and re-mine the belt, the difference between a breach held for an hour and a breach the enemy cannot re-close at all.

complications.name: Lane Integrity Is Everything
complications.text: The decisive thing in the belt is not ground taken but lanes kept open. A few narrow cleared paths carry the whole force through; everything off them is mines and ditches and death. A lane suppressed by fire, re-mined, or blocked by a wreck is a closed lane, and a closed lane strands every unit relying on it. The operation is measured in open lanes, not in kilometers.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Track the status of each cut lane. Units move through the belt only on open lanes. A lane suppressed by fire, re-mined, or blocked by wreckage is closed until reopened. Off-lane belt hexes are mined and ditched, halting and damaging any unit that enters. Lane count and status govern the rate at which the force can pass through.

complications.name: The Re-Seal
complications.text: {NPC:opfor-commander}'s plan is to let force through and then close the lanes behind it. Engineer teams re-mine the cleared paths, fresh fire drops on the gaps, and the belt seals with friendly units stranded on the far side. The danger is not being stopped at the wire; it is being let through and then cut off, trapped between a re-closed obstacle field and the defense beyond.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The defender attempts to re-seal lanes after units have passed through them, using re-mining teams and suppressing fire. A lane re-sealed behind units that crossed strands them on the far side of the belt, cut off from support and reinforcement. Preventing the re-seal requires holding the lane mouths and suppressing the obstacle-control positions.

complications.name: Fire Into the Obstacles
complications.text: The guns covering the belt are positioned to fire into the obstacles, not over them — laid on the ditches and the minefields and the likely breach sites, where a bogged-down or funneled 'Mech is a fixed target. The engineers cut the lanes under that fire, and the units filing through are funneled into the exact ground the defender has ranged.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The belt's covering guns are pre-ranged on the obstacles and the likely lane sites. Units in the lanes and engineers at the breach take concentrated fire while confined to the cut paths. Suppressing or destroying the covering positions reduces the fire on the lanes; until then, every passage runs through pre-ranged ground.

complications.name: Counterattack on the Breach
complications.text: The defender keeps a mobile element to counterattack the breach sites, hitting the lane mouths while the force is half through, throwing the passage into confusion, and buying time for the re-seal. A breach in progress is most vulnerable at the gaps, where the assault is funneled and the engineers are exposed.
complications.mechanicalEffect: A mobile reserve counterattacks the breach sites at the timeline mark, striking the lane mouths to disrupt the passage and cover the re-seal. Holding the lane mouths against it is required to keep the lanes open. A counterattack that reaches a breach site closes that lane and strands the units relying on it.

decisionPoints.name: Cutting the Belt
decisionPoints.context: The belt has to become lanes, and the lanes have to hold. You have three options. Cut many thin lanes and pass the force quickly across a wide front — harder for the enemy to re-seal all at once, but each one lightly held. Cut a few wide, deep lanes — easy to hold, but a narrow funnel everything must use. Or feint lanes across the belt while the real breach goes in concentrated, splitting the defender's re-seal effort. Each option trades how fast the force passes against how surely the lanes hold.

options.title: Many Thin Lanes
advantages: Many thin lanes across a wide front pass the force quickly and give the defender too many gaps to re-seal at once
No single lane is a chokepoint — losing one does not strand the whole force
disadvantages: Each thin lane is lightly held and easily suppressed or re-mined individually
Spreading the engineers and the covering force across many breaches leaves each one weak against a focused counterattack
options.consequence: You pass the force quickly across a wide front and dare the enemy to close them all, but each lane is fragile. He cannot re-seal every gap, but he can pick off the weakest, and a force spread across many lanes holds none of them strongly.

costs.resource: The engineers and covering force spread thin across many breach sites, each lightly held
costs.risk: The defender re-seals the weakest lanes one by one and counterattacks the thinnest mouths — fast passage across gaps too fragile to all hold

options.title: Few Wide Lanes
advantages: A small number of wide, well-cleared lanes are held in strength and hard to re-seal or suppress
Concentrates the covering force on a few breach sites that stay open against the counterattack
disadvantages: Few lanes funnel the whole force through narrow fronts — slow passage and a concentrated target
If the defender does close one of the few lanes, a large share of the force is stranded or stalled
options.consequence: You hold the lanes you cut and pass the force through them surely, but slowly, and through a funnel the defender knows exactly where to range. The lanes stay open, and everything depends on the few of them not failing.

costs.resource: The whole force funneled through a few wide lanes — slow passage through pre-ranged, concentrated ground
costs.risk: A defender who closes even one of the few lanes strands a large share of the force — sure lanes, but catastrophic if one fails

options.title: Feint Lanes, Breach Concentrated
advantages: Engineer activity feinted across the belt draws the defender's re-seal and fire to false breaches while the real lanes go in concentrated
Splits the defender's limited re-seal capacity away from the lanes that matter
disadvantages: Mounting feint breaches spends engineer effort and covering force on lanes never meant to carry the force
A defender who sees through the feint concentrates his re-seal on the real breach and meets it with his full effort
options.consequence: You buy the real lanes time by giving the defender false ones to chase, at the cost of effort spent on breaches that lead nowhere. Sold well, the force passes through lanes he is not watching; seen through, the real breach meets his whole re-seal undivided.

costs.resource: Engineer effort and covering force spent on feint breaches to draw off the defender's re-seal
costs.risk: A defender who sees through the feint throws his full re-seal at the real breach — effort wasted on false lanes and the true one met undivided

entries.event: The covering force opens fire and the engineers begin cutting lanes into the belt. The obstacle's covering guns fire into the breach sites.
The first lanes are cleared and the lead units begin filing through. {NPC:opfor-commander} reads the breach points and orders the re-seal prepared.
The mobile reserve counterattacks the breach sites. Re-mining teams move to close the lanes behind the units already through.
The decisive phase: the lanes are held open and the heavy units pass through, or the re-seal closes them with force stranded in and beyond the belt.
The heavy units are through onto the open ground and the breach is held, or the lanes are sealed and whatever crossed is trapped on the far side of the belt.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: The lanes must be held open and the heavy units passed through before the defender's re-seal closes them, by roughly T+20:00. Lanes sealed with the force half through strand whatever crossed on the far side of the belt, between a re-closed obstacle field and the defense beyond. The breach then becomes a trap that has to be re-opened from the wrong side.

opforSketch.composition: An obstacle-belt defense built around the belt itself: a 'Mech force of mediums and heavies (45-80 tons) at Regular quality in positions sited to fire into the obstacles, reinforced by dug-in fixed guns pre-ranged on the breach sites and combat-engineer teams for re-mining and re-sealing the lanes. A mobile 'Mech reserve, Regular-to-Veteran quality, counterattacks the breach sites, supported by a fast armor element (Pegasus and hover behavior) to harass the lane mouths. The belt's obstacle-control post coordinates the re-seal.
opforSketch.behavior: Obstacle-defense doctrine: fight the lanes rather than the assault. Cover the breach sites with pre-ranged fire, let force through and then re-seal the lanes behind it to strand it, and counterattack the breach mouths to disrupt the passage and buy time for the re-seal. The fixed positions fire into the obstacles to destruction. The mobile reserve and the engineer teams work to close the gaps, timing the re-seal to trap the most force on the far side of the belt.

forks.name: OPERATION OPEN GROUND
forks.trigger: The lanes were held open and the heavy units passed through the belt onto the open ground beyond. The obstacle field is breached and held.
forks.consequence: The trap has sprung the wrong way for the enemy. The belt is breached, the lanes are open, and the heavy units are through onto the ground he filled with obstacles to deny. The order is to push off the breach into the open country beyond before the defender can fall back to a new line. Your force drives through the held lanes into the open. The lane is clear; now the force runs through it.

forks.name: OPERATION SEALED BELT
forks.trigger: The defender re-sealed the lanes with force on the far side. Units are stranded in and beyond the belt, cut off behind a re-closed obstacle field.
forks.consequence: The belt closed behind the lead units, exactly as the defender planned, and part of the force is trapped on the far side between the obstacles and the defense. The next operation is to re-open a lane from the near side and extract the stranded units before they are destroyed in the belt — a second breach, made under worse conditions, to undo the trap the first one walked into. The belt sealed; the trapped force must be recovered. The lane closed; it is cut again.

storyElementSeed: An engineer team clears a path through a minefield on hands and knees under fire, marking the lane meter by meter with tape and lamps. Behind them a column of 'Mechs waits nose-to-tail for a road being made one careful pace at a time. A sergeant counts the gaps still left to clear.

is-davion.objectives.primary: Cut clear lanes through the obstacle belt under fire and keep them open against the enemy's re-seal, passing the heavy units through to the open ground beyond. The lanes are the battle; hold them or be sealed inside the belt.

is-marik.objectives.primary: Breach the deep obstacle belt with cut lanes and hold them open while the heavy units pass, keeping the gaps clear of the enemy's re-mining and fire. Command wants the belt forced and the force through — not half of it stranded behind a re-closed field.

LANE_COUNT.unit: lanes to be cut and held

inspiration: A long-range strike to sever an enemy's communications nerve at a chosen moment — cutting the cables and relays that carry the high command's traffic so a region goes deaf exactly when the main blow lands, where the relay is hardened and the silence has to fall on a timetable, not just eventually.
skeleton: a deep raiding element must reach and wreck a hardened long-range communications relay so an occupied region falls deaf at one chosen hour to cover a separate main effort, where the relay is buried and guarded and a partial strike only delays the traffic rather than killing it, and the raid must put the silence on a fixed timetable then get clear before the garrison's reaction force arrives, so the crux is timing a clean total cut against a hardened node rather than merely damaging it and escaping the blackout it creates
title: OPERATION DEAF PROVINCE
situation: The whole province on {WORLD} depends on one relay for its orders, and {EMPLOYER} wants it dead at a particular hour and not before. The occupation routes its long-range command traffic for the {DISTRICT} sector through a single hardened communications station. It is a buried signal hall under a reinforced cap on high ground. The dishes and the trunk lines feeding it are the only soft parts of an otherwise armored node. Cut it, and the sector's garrisons lose contact with each other and with high command for as long as it takes to rig a replacement. They cannot coordinate or call for help. A separate main effort elsewhere is timed to land during that silence, and that is the whole point. The relay does not need to die early. It needs to die on the hour and stay dead long enough to matter. {NPC:intel-source} has the station mapped: the dish field, the trunk conduits, the buried hall, and the relief schedule. But the intelligence is {INTEL_AGE_DAYS} days old, and the conduits may have been re-routed or hardened since. So the team must confirm on the ground that the cut is total, not trust the plan. A partial strike is the failure that looks like success. Destroy the dishes but leave the buried trunk, and the traffic reroutes within the hour. The silence collapses, and the main effort lands in a sector that can still talk.
