A raid that wants the files intact must prevent both the convoy's departure and the escort's own attempt to destroy them, not merely take the building.

complications.name: Channeled City Ground
complications.text: The building sits in dense city ground. The convoy's route out runs through narrow streets a raid can block, but where a 'Mech is visible and cramped. Cutting the convoy's road is possible, but it commits force to the streets. The same narrow ground that lets the raiders block the evacuation lets the escort hold them off the building.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The urban ground restricts maneuver and exposes 'Mechs at a distance; the convoy route can be cut at chokepoints, but doing so divides the raiding force between the building and the streets. The narrow terrain helps both blocking the evacuation and defending the archive, depending on who holds which chokepoint.

decisionPoints.name: Beating the Evacuation
decisionPoints.context: The convoy is loading and the strong-room is the prize. How to beat the evacuation is the choice. Drive straight for the strong-room to reach the files before they are boxed and gone. Or cut the convoy's route out first, to trap the archive at the building and take it at leisure. Or split the force, blocking the road while a party drives for the files, racing both the loading and the escort at once.

options.title: Drive for the Strong-Room
advantages: Goes straight for the files before the loading can finish: the most direct way to reach the archive while it is still there
Reaches the carry-or-burn choice fastest, before the convoy can leave with the prize
disadvantages: Leaving the convoy route open means a load already on the trucks may drive out the back while the team takes the strong-room
A direct drive meets the escort at its strongest, where it is covering the archive itself
options.consequence: You reach the files fastest and make the choice at the strong-room in time, but the part of the archive already loaded may escape up an open road while you fight for the part still inside; the prize half-taken and half-gone.

costs.resource: the convoy route left open while the team drives for the building
costs.risk: A load already on the trucks drives out the open road while the team takes the strong-room; the archive split, half seized and half evacuated

options.title: Cut the Convoy's Road First
advantages: Traps the whole archive at the building by blocking the route out; nothing can be evacuated once the road is cut
Turns the race against the convoy into a fight for a building that cannot send its prize away
disadvantages: Cutting the road first spends time and force on the streets while the loading continues and the escort digs in at the archive
An escort whose convoy is blocked knows it cannot evacuate and may turn to destroying the archive itself
options.consequence: You make sure nothing leaves by cutting the road, but the delay lets the escort prepare the building's defense and, knowing the files cannot go, perhaps burn them rather than give them up; the archive trapped and maybe burned by its own keepers.

costs.resource: the time and force spent cutting the road while the escort fortifies and the loading continues
costs.risk: An escort that cannot evacuate the trapped archive destroys it itself; the convoy stopped and the files burned by the very hand the raid meant to take them from

options.title: Split — Block and Seize
advantages: Blocks the convoy route and drives for the strong-room at once, racing both the loading and the escape together
Hedges against the archive being loaded out the back while the building is taken
disadvantages: Dividing the force puts a thin party at the strong-room against the escort's strongest point and a thin block on the road
Neither the block nor the assault on the building is at full strength, and the escort may break through one or the other
options.consequence: You cover both the road and the room by splitting up, and if both halves hold, the whole archive is yours; but a divided raid is thin everywhere, and the escort may break the block to run the convoy or break the assault to save the files.

costs.resource: the raid divided between blocking the road and seizing the building, thin at both
costs.risk: A split raid the escort breaks through at one point loses either the block, and the convoy runs, or the assault, and the building holds; thin everywhere and decisive nowhere

entries.event: The raid reaches the archive's district; the evacuation is already loading and the convoy forming up, with the {INTEL_AGE_HOURS}-hour-old schedule the only indication of how far along it is.
The team commits to its approach; the escort covers the loading and the strong-room as the raid develops its attack.
The strong-room is reached or the convoy nears readiness; the carry-or-burn choice is forced as the pressure of the evacuation peaks.
{NPC:opfor-commander}'s reaction force beyond the escort closes on the district; the team must have the files taken or burned and be withdrawing.
The reaction force arrives; an archive not yet seized or destroyed has either left for the rear or is being burned by its own escort, and a team still at the building is pinned down.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: Reach the archive and either seize or destroy it before the convoy departs and before {NPC:opfor-commander}'s reaction force arrives around T+16:00. A convoy that leaves first carries the resistance's names to the secure rear. An escort that knows it is losing may burn the files first. A team still at the building when the reaction force closes in is pinned down in city ground, around a strong-room it did not empty in time.

opforSketch.composition: A secret-police security force and evacuation escort plus a city reaction force. The archive is held by a security detachment with a light-'Mech section (20-40 tons), and the evacuation escort is a mobile column of light and medium 'Mechs (25-50 tons) and an armor section (Goblin infantry carriers and Scorpion light tanks) forming up to convoy the files out, at Regular quality. Beyond them is {NPC:opfor-commander}'s on-call reaction force, a company (slightly under strength) of medium 'Mechs (40-55 tons) at Regular-to-Veteran quality. Counter-intelligence officers at the strong-room are non-combatants but will burn the archive if ordered.
opforSketch.behavior: Evacuation-escort doctrine: the escort's first aim is to get the archive away, covering the loading and fighting to get the convoy moving rather than to hold the building. Blocked from evacuating, it switches to denial, destroying the archive itself rather than let it be captured intact. The security detachment defends the strong-room from prepared positions; the reaction force drives for the district to pin the raiders down. The escort values the files leaving or burning over its own survival; the reaction force presses to trap the raid at the building before it can withdraw with the prize.

forks.name: OPERATION CLEAN SLATE
forks.trigger: The archive was reached before the convoy departed and either seized intact or destroyed in place; the resistance's names did not reach the secure rear.
forks.consequence: The files did not get away. Taken or burned, the occupation's picture of the resistance is gone, and the cells on {WORLD} are safe from the roundup that archive would have enabled. If the files were taken intact, the order is to act on the counter-intelligence they hold: a strike to roll up the collaborator network the archive named, before the occupation realizes its own files now serve the other side. The slate is clean; now the hunt turns around.

forks.name: OPERATION OPEN BOOK
forks.trigger: The convoy left before the raid reached the strong-room, or the reaction force pinned the team down at the building; the archive reached the secure rear or the raid is trapped.
forks.consequence: The archive got away to the rear, or the team is pinned down at the building with the reaction force closing in and the files still inside. Either way the resistance is exposed: the occupation has, or will soon have, the names and cell maps to roll up the network on {WORLD}. The next operation is to break the team clear and to warn and scatter the compromised cells before the secret police can act on the captured files. The files escaped; the resistance runs.

storyElementSeed: In a strong-room lined with file drawers, a raider holds an incendiary charge in one hand and a single pulled folder in the other. She is reading a collaborator list that would let the resistance turn the whole hunt around. Down the corridor the loading-bay doors roll open, and an officer's voice orders the convoy to start engines. The choice between burning the archive and carrying the files off has about a minute left to make.

is-liao.objectives.primary: Reach the archive before the convoy leaves and either take the files or burn them; the names must not reach the rear. Better the counter-intelligence in our hands than ash, but ash before the enemy keeps them, every time.

is-davion.objectives.primary: Reach the strong-room before the evacuation leaves and either carry the archive off or destroy it in place, denying the occupation the resistance's names. Take the files if you can hold them, burn them if you cannot, but do not let them reach the rear intact.

FILE_HAUL_TONS.unit: tons of archive to carry off

inspiration: A pathfinder mission to mark a target for a precision strike: a small team must work close to a hardened automated defence site, place and hold a designation on it through the strike's run-in, and survive the dwell — where the mark is everything, the automated net relocates its mobile elements if it detects the team before the strike lands, and the strike's own fall is a danger to the markers.
skeleton: a pathfinder team must infiltrate close to a hardened automated planetary-defence site, place a target designation on it, and hold that mark unbroken through the run-in of a separate orbital or aerospace strike, where the designation must be sustained through a timed window rather than merely planted, the automated net relocates its mobile defences if it detects the team before the strike arrives, and the strike's own impact endangers the markers, so the crux is holding the mark through the dwell under a tireless sensor net rather than reaching the site or destroying it directly
title: OPERATION STEADY LIGHT
situation: The strike meant to destroy the defense site on {WORLD} cannot find it without you. The occupation runs a hardened automated planetary-defense installation in {DISTRICT}. It is a buried, armored complex of fixed gun batteries and caretaker units. No ground force in the theater can take it out. But a precision strike from above can break it, if the strike knows exactly where to fall. Knowing exactly where is the problem. The site is hardened against observation from orbit, its targets buried and hidden among decoys. A strike fired on a survey guess scatters harmlessly off armor and decoys. So a pathfinder team goes in to mark it. The team puts a laser designator's mark on the real targets and holds that mark steady through the strike's approach, so the fire falls where it must. Holding the mark is the whole mission. {NPC:intel-source} has the approaches and the sensor coverage mapped: the gaps in the sensor network's sweep and the hidden vantage point from which a designator can see the targets. But he warns the intel is {INTEL_AGE_HOURS} hours old, and the sweep timing may have shifted since. So the team must read the sweep on the ground. The hard part is not placing the mark. It is holding it. The mark has to stay on the target through the strike's approach window. That means minutes of steady laser-marking from a team sitting still and close while a tireless sensor network sweeps the ground around it. And the network does not just catch intruders. It relocates its defenses. If the complex detects the team before the strike lands, it shifts its mobile elements, and the strike falls on positions already abandoned. The mark is held perfectly on a target that has moved. {NPC:opfor-commander} oversees the site and keeps a mobile response force beyond the automated network to deal with anything it flags. There is one last danger. The strike the team calls down falls close. The team has to hold the mark through the approach and then survive the impact they guided in. The ground is broken high country and open dust: long sightlines for the designator and little cover for the team holding it. Recommended force: {FORCE_SIZE}, kept light. Place the mark, hold it steady through the window, and ride out the strike. Lose the mark and the strike is wasted. Be seen before it lands and the site you marked is no longer there.

objectives.primary: Infiltrate to the designation vantage point and place a mark on the defense site's real targets. Hold it unbroken through the strike's approach window, so the precision strike falls where it must. Then survive the impact and withdraw.
objectives.secondary: Stay undetected by the automated sensor network until the strike lands. A team flagged before the fire falls causes the complex to relocate its mobile defenses, and the strike then breaks empty positions instead of the site.
objectives.bonus: Mark a second target (the site's buried fire-control center or power feed) within the same window, so the strike destroys not just the visible gun batteries but the core systems that would let the complex be rebuilt.

complications.name: Holding the Mark
complications.text: Placing the designation is quick. Holding it is the mission. The mark has to stay on the target through the strike's approach window: minutes of a team sitting still and exposed, the laser steady, while every instinct says move. A mark that breaks partway through the approach sends the strike wide. The discipline of holding still through that wait is the whole job.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The designation must be held on the target through the strike's approach window; the team holds position and keeps the mark unbroken for the required duration. Breaking the mark early (by moving, by losing line of sight, by being driven off) scatters the strike and fails the primary objective. This is a fixed, exposed wait, not an instant action.

complications.name: The Net Relocates
complications.text: The automated complex does not just try to catch the team. It responds to detection by moving. If the network flags the pathfinders before the strike lands, the site shifts its mobile defensive elements off their marked positions, and the strike falls on ground they have left. A mark held perfectly is worth nothing if the thing it marks has moved away.
complications.mechanicalEffect: If the automated network detects the team before the strike's impact, the site relocates its mobile elements; the strike then falls on abandoned positions, sharply reducing its effect even with the mark held. Staying undetected through the entire wait, not merely placing the mark, is what makes the strike land on a target that is still there.

complications.name: The Tireless Sweep
complications.text: The network's sensors sweep the ground on a cycle that never tires and never lets up, and the vantage point that sees the targets is within that sweep's reach. The team has to place and hold the mark in the gaps of a sweep cycle that does not stop, reading a rhythm that may have shifted since the intelligence was taken.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The automated sensor sweep runs on a timing cycle the team must read and work within; holding the mark means staying in the sweep's gaps through the wait. The timing may differ from the {INTEL_AGE_HOURS}-hour-old report, requiring the team to confirm it on the ground and raising the detection risk if they misjudge it.

complications.name: Under Your Own Fire
complications.text: The strike the team calls down falls close to the vantage point that guides it. The team holds the laser on target through the approach and then has to ride out the impact they aimed in. A precision strike is precise, but close is still close, and the team that brought the fire down is near enough to feel it.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The strike's impact endangers the team's position; holding the mark to the last second of the approach maximizes the strike's accuracy but keeps the team closest to the impact. A vantage point chosen for the best line of sight is also the one nearest the danger zone, trading designation quality against the team's own safety at impact.

decisionPoints.name: Where to Hold the Light
decisionPoints.context: The mark must be held through the strike's approach, and where the team holds it sets the whole gamble. Take the close vantage point with the cleanest line for the surest mark, nearest the sensor network and the impact; take a distant vantage point that trades mark quality for staying outside the sweep and the blast; or split up, with one marker forward at the close vantage point and the rest of the team back, holding the mark with fewer people but keeping the rest safer.

options.title: Close Hide, Surest Mark
advantages: The cleanest line of sight to the targets: the steadiest, most accurate designation through the approach
A close mark is the hardest for the site to decoy and the most likely to put the strike dead on target
disadvantages: The close vantage point is deepest inside the network's sweep, the highest chance of detection during the long wait
It is also nearest the impact, so the team rides out its own strike at close range
options.consequence: You get the surest mark and the best strike, but you hold it from inside the sweep and under the impact. Detection before impact relocates the target, and the close vantage point puts the team in the blast: the best designation on the worst ground for the team.

costs.resource: the team holds the mark deep in the sweep and close to the impact for the surest designation
costs.risk: A close vantage point caught mid-wait relocates the target and rides out its own strike at close range; the best mark held from the most dangerous ground

options.title: Distant Hide, Safer Dwell
advantages: A vantage point outside the network's tightest sweep: a far lower chance of detection during the approach wait
Distance from the impact lets the team ride out the strike safely
disadvantages: A distant mark is less precise and easier for the site to spoof with decoys; the strike may scatter even with the mark held
The longer range to the targets makes the designation harder to hold steady through the window
options.consequence: You hold the mark from safer ground and survive the strike easily, but the distant designation is the one the site can spoil. The strike may fall off the decoyed targets despite a mark held the whole window: the safest wait but the least reliable mark.

costs.resource: the mark's precision traded for distance from the sweep and the blast
costs.risk: A distant, less precise mark lets the site spoof the strike off target with decoys; the mark held the whole window and the fire scattered anyway

options.title: Split — Marker Forward, Team Back
advantages: A single marker at the close vantage point holds the surest mark while the rest of the team stays back, out of the sweep and the blast
Hedges the accurate mark against keeping most of the team safe
disadvantages: The forward marker holds the mark alone, deep in the sweep, with no one near to cover or pull them out if flagged
A split team is thin if the mobile response force arrives, the marker isolated forward and the rest too far to help quickly
options.consequence: You get the close vantage point's accurate mark with most of the team out of danger, but the marker holds it alone in the sweep and under the impact. If flagged or caught, the forward marker is on their own: the surest mark bought with one person's exposure.

costs.resource: a lone marker forward in the sweep and the blast while the team holds back
costs.risk: The isolated forward marker is flagged or caught with no one near to help; the accurate mark held at the cost of a marker the team cannot reach in time

entries.event: The team infiltrates to the designation vantage point and reads the network's sweep timing against the {INTEL_AGE_HOURS}-hour-old plan; the targets are acquired.
The mark is placed on the real targets; the strike's approach window opens and the team begins the wait, holding the laser steady in the sweep's gaps.
The strike makes its approach; the team holds the mark unbroken to the last second, and the fire falls on the marked targets, provided the network has not flagged the team and relocated the target.
The strike impacts; the team rides out the fire it guided in and {NPC:opfor-commander}'s mobile response force launches toward the site.
The mobile response force closes on the area; the team must be clear of the vantage point and withdrawing through the broken ground.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: Hold the mark unbroken through the approach to the strike's impact around T+6:00. Stay undetected until the fire falls, and be clear of the vantage point before the mobile response force arrives around T+15:00. A mark broken partway through the approach scatters the strike. A team flagged before impact watches the strike break empty positions the site relocated to. A team still at the vantage point when the response force closes in is caught on open ground beside the site it marked.

opforSketch.composition: A hardened automated defense site plus a mobile response force. The complex itself is a buried installation of fixed automated gun batteries and caretaker units (light and medium automated 'Mechs, 25-50 tons, and fixed guns) with relocatable mobile defensive elements, no morale, controlled by a tireless sensor network. The decisive human force is {NPC:opfor-commander}'s on-call mobile response force, a company (slightly under strength) of medium 'Mechs (40-55 tons) at Regular-to-Veteran quality with a fast armor section (Saladin tank destroyers and hovercraft), which launches on anything the network flags. The site's mobile elements reposition on detection.
opforSketch.behavior: Automated-defense doctrine: the sensor network sweeps the ground relentlessly and responds to detecting an intruder by repositioning the site's mobile defensive elements off their known positions, defeating a guided strike by moving the target. The fixed batteries and caretakers attack on contact and fight to the death with no morale. The mobile response force drives for any flagged contact to hunt the pathfinders down on the open ground; it presses hard once the network has a fix, valuing the destruction of the team before they can withdraw. The automated elements never break; the response force breaks off only once the area is cleared.

forks.name: OPERATION CLEAN STRIKE
forks.trigger: The mark was held unbroken through the approach, the team undetected until impact, and the strike broke the defense site on the real targets.
forks.consequence: The strike fell where it had to and the hardened site that no ground force could take out is broken open. The order is to exploit the gap the strike tore in the occupation's defenses: a follow-on ground operation through the now-silenced defensive belt before the enemy can rebuild or reposition to cover the hole. The mark held; the fire fell true; now the door is open.

forks.name: OPERATION WASTED FIRE
forks.trigger: The mark broke partway through the approach, or the team was flagged and the site relocated, or the response force caught the team; the strike scattered or fell on empty positions.
forks.consequence: The strike was wasted (the mark lost, or the target moved out from under it, or the team caught before the fire fell) and the hardened site still stands, now alert and with its mobile elements repositioned. The next operation is to break the team clear of the area and salvage the mission: a second marking attempt under a sensor network now on alert, or an extraction from a site that knows it was almost destroyed. The fire fell wide; the team runs.

storyElementSeed: A scout lies prone behind a laser designator on a ridge of broken rock, holding the crosshair dead steady on a bunker opening. A sensor mast on the site below sweeps past the ridge and away. He counts down the seconds of the strike's approach under his breath. The fire he is calling in will land close enough to throw grit over him when it comes.

is-davion.objectives.primary: Get a mark on the site's real targets and hold it dead steady through the strike's approach, then ride out the impact and get clear. Holding the mark is the mission: hold it through the window or the strike is wasted, and stay unseen or the target moves.

is-steiner.objectives.primary: Place and hold a designation on the defense site's targets through the strike window so the fire falls true, then withdraw. Hold the mark and stay undetected until impact; a strike fired at a relocated target is ordnance spent for nothing.

inspiration: A single-night railway interdiction to freeze a specific reinforcement move: multiple independent demolition teams must cut a transport network's switches and bridges in the same narrow window so a reinforcing force cannot make a coming move, where the teams cannot coordinate by radio, every cut must land inside the window, and a single missed cut leaves a route open that defeats the whole effort.
skeleton: multiple independent demolition teams must cut a transport network's key switches and bridges within one synchronized window to freeze a specific enemy reinforcement move during a coming operation, where the teams cannot coordinate once committed and each must land its cut inside the window on its own clock, a single uncut route left open lets the reinforcement through and defeats the whole effort, and the cuts must be timed to the move rather than made early, so the crux is synchronizing independent severances with no comms so the network fails all at once rather than piecemeal
title: OPERATION ONE NIGHT
situation: A separate SLDF operation is about to land in {DISTRICT} on {WORLD}. The occupier will answer it by rushing reinforcements down the sector's transport network. That network is the rail and road lines that carry heavy units forward from the rear. Your job is to make the whole network fail in one night so those reinforcements cannot move. If they cannot move, the SLDF operation faces only the enemy already there. The network has more than one route, and that is the catch. Cut every route but one and you have done nothing, because the reinforcements just take the route still open. So this is a timed interdiction. Several independent demolition teams will destroy the network's chokepoints. Chokepoints are the switches, junctions, and bridges that cannot be quickly bypassed. Every cut must land inside one narrow time window. {NPC:intel-source} has mapped the network and picked the chokepoints that strand the most traffic for the longest. Their read on enemy repair crews and patrols is {INTEL_AGE_DAYS} days old, so the guard on the key bridges may be heavier now. The timing is the hard part. Once the teams move in, they cannot talk to each other. Any radio call can be traced by direction-finding and get a team killed. So each team carries its own clock to its own chokepoint. Each one blows its charges inside the window on its own judgment and trusts the rest to do the same. A network that fails all at once is frozen and cannot be rerouted. A network that fails one cut at a time is just repaired and bypassed gap by gap. The cuts must also land on time, not early. A bridge blown a day too soon lets the occupier reroute and repair before it matters. {NPC:opfor-commander} commands the sector and keeps mobile patrols and engineer-repair units. They rush to any cut the moment it is reported. The ground is open farmland cut by the rivers the bridges span. Recommended force: {FORCE_SIZE}, split into independent teams. Destroy every chokepoint inside the window, all at once, and the reinforcements are frozen out. Miss one cut, or spread the cuts across the night, and the network still carries them through.

objectives.primary: Destroy every assigned chokepoint of the transport network within the one timed window. That means the switches, junctions, and bridges. Do this so the occupier's reinforcements cannot reach {DISTRICT} during the coming SLDF operation.
objectives.secondary: Land all the cuts together, not one at a time. A network cut all at once cannot be rerouted. But if the cuts come one by one, the occupier repairs and bypasses each gap as fast as it appears, and the network keeps working.
objectives.bonus: Destroy the network's main repair-train marshalling yard along with the chokepoints. This denies the occupier the means to repair the cuts quickly and extends the shutdown from hours into days.

complications.name: No Comms Once Committed
complications.text: The teams go in under radio silence and stay silent, because any transmission can be located by direction-finding and would get the team killed. Once they move in, no team knows whether the others have reached their chokepoints or been captured. Each carries its own clock and must set off its charges on time, trusting the rest to do the same. The synchronization depends entirely on each team's own timing.
complications.mechanicalEffect: After the teams move in, they have no communication with each other; each must detonate within the window using only its own timing. No team can confirm the others' status or adjust for a teammate's delay or loss. The synchronized failure succeeds only if every team independently hits the window.

complications.name: One Open Route Defeats It
complications.text: The network has more than one route, and that is the whole difficulty. Destroy every chokepoint but one and the reinforcement simply uses the route still open. The mission is all-or-nothing, because a single working route carries the force through. Every team's cut matters absolutely, and if any one team fails, the entire effort fails.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The reinforcement is stopped only if all assigned chokepoints are destroyed within the window. A single uncut route lets the force through and fails the primary objective, no matter how many other cuts succeeded. There is no partial credit: the network fails completely or, in practical terms, not at all.

complications.name: On Time, Not Early
complications.text: The cuts are timed to the reinforcement's move. A cut made too early is undone before it counts. Destroy a chokepoint a day ahead and the occupier reroutes, repairs, and adapts before the SLDF operation lands. The window is not just about the teams striking together. It is about striking at the moment the shutdown actually blocks the move.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Cuts made before the synchronized window give the occupier time to reroute and repair before the operation. The shutdown must coincide with the reinforcement move to stop it. Early cuts reduce the effect even if all chokepoints are eventually destroyed.

complications.name: The Repair Converges
complications.text: {NPC:opfor-commander} keeps mobile patrols and engineer-repair units. They rush to any reported cut to guard the gap and start repairs. A team that lingers at a wrecked chokepoint draws that response onto itself. So does a team whose cut is reported before the others land. And a guarded chokepoint under repair does not stay shut for long.
complications.mechanicalEffect: When a cut is reported, mobile patrol and repair elements converge on that chokepoint; teams that linger are engaged, and repairs begin, shortening the shutdown. A cut reported early (out of sync) draws the response before the other cuts land, increasing the chance the synchronization breaks down.

decisionPoints.name: Timing the Net's Failure
decisionPoints.context: Every team must hit the window. The choice is how to time the failure. Option one: set a single exact moment that all teams cut to. It is sharp, but leaves no room for a team running late. Option two: set a short tolerance window of a few minutes for all cuts to fall within. It is more forgiving, but it gives the occupier those few minutes of warning between the first cut and the last. Option three: stagger the cuts by route priority. Destroy the fastest, highest-capacity routes first, so even a late cut on a slow route still stops the reinforcement.

options.title: One Hard Moment
advantages: All cuts happen at one instant — the network fails completely and at once, with no warning between chokepoints
The occupier gets no time to react to a first cut before the rest land
disadvantages: No margin for error — a single team that misses the moment leaves its route open and defeats the whole effort
Demands perfect independent timing from every team, with no allowance for a slow approach or a guarded bridge
options.consequence: If every team hits the exact moment, you get the cleanest, most complete shutdown. But the plan has no margin. One team delayed by a patrol or a hard approach leaves a route open, and the network carries the reinforcement through.

costs.resource: all margin spent on demanding a single perfectly synchronized instant from every team
costs.risk: One team that misses the exact moment leaves its route open and defeats the entire interdiction — the network fails everywhere except the one place that mattered

options.title: A Short Tolerance Window
advantages: A few-minute band for all cuts to fall within — forgiving of a team running slightly late
Far likelier that every chokepoint is actually destroyed, achieving the all-or-nothing shutdown
disadvantages: The gap between the first cut and the last gives the occupier minutes of warning to start rerouting
A reported first cut brings the repair response in before the last cuts land
options.consequence: Allowing a margin makes the full shutdown far likelier. But that margin is also warning. The occupier learns the network is being cut at the first chokepoint and starts reacting before the last one falls. It is a surer shutdown, but one that announces itself.

costs.resource: the warning given to the occupier in the minutes between the first cut and the last
costs.risk: The tolerance band warns the occupier from the first cut; the repair response moves in and rerouting begins before the last chokepoints are destroyed

options.title: Stagger by Route Priority
advantages: Destroys the fastest, highest-capacity routes first, so the most dangerous routes are shut down earliest
A late cut on a slow secondary route still stops the reinforcement, because the fast routes are already gone
disadvantages: A deliberate stagger gives the clearest warning and the most time for the occupier to react to the early cuts
Staggering means the network is never fully down at once until the last cut — a window in which the slow routes are still passable
options.consequence: You guarantee the dangerous fast routes fail first, and you gain some slack on the slow ones. But the deliberate sequence is the loudest warning, and it leaves the secondary routes open the longest. You kill the reinforcement's fast options early, at the cost of a slow leak and a tipped hand.

costs.resource: the early warning and the slow-route leak accepted in order to guarantee the fast routes fail first
costs.risk: The staggered sequence warns the occupier early and leaves slow routes open longest — the reinforcement delayed and degraded rather than stopped outright

entries.event: The independent teams move in toward their chokepoints and go silent; each carries its own clock toward the synchronized window.
The teams reach their assigned switches, junctions, and bridges and set their charges, each unable to see the others' progress.
The synchronized window opens and the cuts land — together if the timing held, scattered if a team ran late or was caught.
The first reported cut brings {NPC:opfor-commander}'s patrol and repair elements in; teams still at their chokepoints are engaged.
Either the shutdown holds across the whole network, or a route left open carries the reinforcement through and repairs begin closing the gaps.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: Every assigned chokepoint must be destroyed within the timed window around T+6:00. The teams must then clear out before the repair response arrives by T+14:00. A single route left open carries the reinforcement through and fails the mission. Cuts scattered across the night are rerouted and repaired one at a time. A team caught lingering at its chokepoint is fought on open ground, far from support.

opforSketch.composition: A sector security and engineer-repair force: mobile patrols of light and medium 'Mechs (25-50 tons) at Regular quality covering the transport network, a fast armor section (Saladins and hovercraft) able to rush to a reported cut, and engineer-repair units with light security. Key bridges may have a dug-in guard with a fixed gun. The decisive response is {NPC:opfor-commander}'s patrol strength concentrating on cuts as they are reported — roughly a company in total, but spread out across the network. Repair crews are non-combatants under escort.
opforSketch.behavior: This force follows line-of-communication security doctrine: patrol the transport network, and on any reported cut, send mobile elements and repair crews to guard the gap and reopen the route. The response is reactive and spread thin — it cannot be everywhere, and it handles cuts in the order they are reported. A network cut all at once overwhelms it; a network cut one piece at a time is handled gap by gap. Patrols engage any demolition teams found at the chokepoints and fight to pin them. Repair elements work under escort to shorten the shutdown. The force prioritizes reopening the routes over destroying the teams, racing to repair the network the operation needs kept down.

forks.name: OPERATION FROZEN NET
forks.trigger: Every chokepoint was destroyed within the window and the network failed all at once; the reinforcement was kept out of the operation.
forks.consequence: The whole network went down together and the reinforcement could not move. So the SLDF operation faced only the forces already there. The order now is to use that opening. Strike the now-unsupported garrison in {DISTRICT} before the occupier can repair the network and bring the reinforcement forward. The network is down. Land the blow while it stays that way.

forks.name: OPERATION OPEN LINE
forks.trigger: A chokepoint was left undestroyed or the cuts scattered across the night; a route stayed open and the reinforcement moved, or the teams were caught at the bridges.
forks.consequence: Either a route stayed open and the reinforcement used it, or the timing broke and the network was repaired around the scattered gaps. The teams that did land their cuts are now spread across the sector with patrols closing in. The next operation is to recover those teams and get them clear of a network that is now fully alert and guarded. The line stayed open. The teams run home separately.

storyElementSeed: A demolition team leader crouches under a rail bridge. His charges are set and the firing handle is in his grip. He watches the second hand of his watch sweep toward the window's mark. The radio stays silent, because no team is allowed to transmit. He has no way to know if he is about to be the only cut on the whole network, or one of six landing together.

is-davion.objectives.primary: Destroy every chokepoint within the window, all of them together, and keep the reinforcement out of the operation. The network only stays cut if it fails all at once. Leave one route open and the whole night was for nothing.

is-marik.objectives.primary: Destroy the transport network's chokepoints within the timed window, severing every assigned route together, so the reinforcement cannot reach {DISTRICT}. Command needs the network shut down for the operation. Do not just drop a handful of bridges and let the trains reroute by dawn.

inspiration: A combat search-and-rescue deep in enemy territory: a recovery team must reach a downed pilot and bring him out before an enemy line-search combing the area converges on the same beacon, where the survivor is mobile but hunted, the beacon that guides the rescue also guides the search, and the comb tightens with every hour.
skeleton: a recovery team must reach a downed friendly aircrew or pilot deep in occupied territory and extract him before an enemy line-search methodically combing the crash area converges on the same beacon, where the survivor is alive and moving but hunted, the beacon that homes the rescue also homes the comb, and the search tightens its net hour by hour, so the crux is reaching the survivor ahead of a converging methodical search and getting both out through the closing comb rather than fighting a fixed garrison
title: OPERATION DOWNED STAR
situation: An SLDF pilot is down and alive deep inside occupied {DISTRICT} on {WORLD}. The enemy is already searching the ground to reach him first. He is a Royal aerospace pilot, and he carries valuable knowledge in his head plus his fighter's flight recorder. He ejected over occupied territory. He is on the ground now, injured but able to move, and transmitting on a recovery beacon. The order is to get him out. Here is the catch: the beacon guiding your rescue is the same beacon guiding the enemy hunt. {NPC:opfor-commander} has launched a slow, careful sweep across the crash area. It is a line of troops and light 'Mechs advancing in formation, homing on the same signal your team is using. It is a race to the pilot, and the searchers started closer. {NPC:intel-source} has the crash area, the beacon's last position, and the shape of the enemy sweep. That means its line of advance and the cordon forming on the far side. But this intel is {INTEL_AGE_HOURS} hours old. A sweep keeps moving, so the picture is already out of date and the net is already tighter than the map shows. The pilot being able to move both helps and hurts. He can move toward you and away from the sweep. But an injured man on the move leaves tracks, and a man transmitting to be found can be found by the searchers too. Your team must reach him ahead of the sweep, take him aboard, and get both out. You face a search closing in from the crash site and a cordon setting up on the likely exit. The enemy commander runs the search slowly and steadily tightens it. This commander also holds a mobile element back to strike the moment the sweep flushes out the pilot or the rescuers. The terrain is close and broken. Jungle and ridges hide the pilot and the searchers alike and slow your approach. Recommended force: {FORCE_SIZE}. Reach the pilot before the sweep does and bring him out through the closing net. Arrive after the search has him and the rescue becomes a prison break. Get boxed in against the cordon and your team joins the hunted.

objectives.primary: Reach the downed pilot ahead of the enemy sweep and take him aboard. Then extract him out of {DISTRICT} through the tightening search and the forming cordon before either closes around him.
objectives.secondary: Reach the pilot before the sweep flushes him out or captures him. A rescue that arrives after the search already has him becomes a prison break. You would be fighting a force that now holds the prize, on far worse terms.
objectives.bonus: Recover the fighter's intelligence recorder from the crash site along with the pilot. The data in the recorder is worth the detour if the sweep has not reached the wreck yet, and worth denying to the enemy in any case.

complications.name: The Beacon Cuts Both Ways
complications.text: The pilot transmits so he can be found, and both sides home on the same signal. The beacon that leads your team to him leads the searchers to him just as well. The longer he transmits, the better the fix both sides get. Switch the beacon off and it hides him from the search and from the rescue at the same time. Leave it on and it guides them both.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The pilot's beacon guides both your team and the enemy sweep. A stronger or longer signal improves both sides' fixes equally. The pilot, or the team once linked up, may switch the beacon off to deny the searchers a fix. But that also kills the recovery's own homing, trading the searchers' track for your own.

complications.name: The Tightening Comb
complications.text: {NPC:opfor-commander}'s search does not rush. It advances in a steady sweep across the crash area, tightening hour by hour, methodical and relentless, with a cordon forming on the far side to catch anyone the sweep flushes out. The recovery team is racing not a reaction force but a closing net, and the net only ever gets smaller.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The enemy sweep advances and tightens on a steady schedule. It shrinks the area where the pilot and the recovery team can move freely, and a cordon forms on the likely exit. The recovery's window narrows the whole time. Every hour the reachable ground and the open exit shrink. A recovery that develops too slowly gets pinned against the cordon.

complications.name: A Hurt Man Moving
complications.text: The pilot can move, but he is injured, and that cuts both ways. He can move toward the recovery and away from the search, but he moves slowly and leaves tracks a skilled tracker can read, and an injured man cannot hide as well as a healthy one. His movement helps the rescue reach him and helps the search find him.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The pilot can reposition toward the recovery or away from the sweep, but slowly, and he leaves a trail that helps the search track him. His injuries limit his speed and endurance; a recovery that takes too long finds a pilot who has been driven by the sweep into worse terrain or has run out of the strength to keep moving.

complications.name: Close and Broken Ground
complications.text: The crash area is jungle and ridges — close terrain that hides the pilot and the searchers alike and slows everything moving through it. The cover that lets the pilot evade is the same cover that lets the search close in unseen, and the broken ground that conceals the recovery team's approach also slows its reach to the pilot and its run to the exit.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The close, broken terrain conceals all parties and slows movement for the recovery team and the sweep alike; 'Mechs are slowed and combat vehicles confined to the few available tracks. The cover helps evasion and ambush equally, and the slow going lengthens both the approach to the pilot and the extraction through the cordon.

decisionPoints.name: Racing the Comb to the Flyer
decisionPoints.context: The pilot is out there transmitting and the search is closing in. The choice is how to win the race. Option one: drive straight and fast for the beacon's fix to beat the search to the pilot. It is loud and quick. Option two: move under cover and slowly to slip inside the search lines unseen. You trade speed for stealth. Option three: have the pilot switch his beacon off and move to a set meeting point. This denies the search its fix, but you lose your own homing too.

options.title: Drive Fast for the Fix
advantages: The quickest way to the pilot — beats the methodical search to him by sheer speed
Reaches the pilot before the tightening net can close around his position
disadvantages: A fast, loud approach draws the search and the mobile element toward the recovery team's track
Speed through the broken ground means less stealth and more tracks for the search to read
options.consequence: You beat the search to the pilot by moving fast, but the speed is loud and pulls the searchers onto the recovery team. You reach the pilot first, then run the extraction with the search already turned toward you.

costs.resource: stealth traded for the speed to beat the search to the pilot
costs.risk: A fast, loud approach pulls the search and the mobile element onto your track. You reach the pilot first, but you run the extraction with the search already closing in

options.title: Move Covered and Slow
advantages: Slips inside the search lines unseen, using the close terrain to reach the pilot without drawing the search
Keeps the recovery team's track hidden so the extraction starts clean
disadvantages: A slow approach may lose the race — the search reaches the pilot's area before the recovery team does
The tightening net may close off the reachable ground while the recovery team is still moving carefully
options.consequence: You stay hidden and start the extraction clean, but the caution spends the same time the search is using to close in. Reach the pilot in time and the rescue is unseen; reach him late and the search has already swept his position.

costs.resource: the time a covered, careful approach spends while the search tightens
costs.risk: A slow approach loses the race. The search reaches the pilot's area first, and the team arrives to a swept position and a closed net

options.title: Cut the Beacon, Meet at a Point
advantages: Switching the beacon off denies the search its fix, blinding the searchers and buying the pilot room
Sends the recovery team and pilot to a prearranged meeting point the search cannot home on
disadvantages: Switching the beacon off blinds the recovery team's homing too. They must find the pilot without the signal, at a point an injured man may not reach
If the pilot cannot make the meeting point, the recovery team has no fix to fall back on
options.consequence: You blind the search by killing the beacon and bet the recovery on a meeting point, denying the searchers their fix but losing your own. If the pilot reaches the point, the rescue slips a blinded search; if he cannot, the recovery team is searching dark ground for a man who never got there.

costs.resource: the recovery team's own homing given up to deny the search the beacon's fix
costs.risk: An injured pilot who cannot reach the meeting point leaves the team searching dark ground with no signal. The search is blinded, and the rescue is blind along with it

entries.event: The recovery team inserts toward the beacon's last position; the enemy sweep is already advancing across the crash area on the same signal.
The team closes on the pilot's area. The sweep has tightened and a cordon is forming on the likely exit. The {INTEL_AGE_HOURS}-hour-old picture is already out of date.
The recovery team reaches the pilot and takes him aboard, or the sweep flushes him out first; the race to the pilot is decided here.
{NPC:opfor-commander}'s mobile element strikes toward the recovery team's track as the extraction starts back through the closing net.
The pilot is out through the search and the cordon, or the recovery team is boxed in against the cordon with the search closing in.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: The pilot must be reached ahead of the sweep and extracted through the tightening net and the forming cordon by around T+18:00. Reach the pilot after the search already has him and you face a prison break against a force holding the prize. Get boxed in against the cordon as the search closes and the team joins the hunted, on broken ground deep in occupied territory.

opforSketch.composition: A search force plus a mobile strike element: the sweep is a dispersed line of motorized infantry and light 'Mechs (20-40 tons) at Regular quality advancing across the crash area, with a cordon of light armor (Goblins and Scorpions) forming on the likely exit. The decisive military element is {NPC:opfor-commander}'s mobile strike force — a reinforced lance to company-minus of medium 'Mechs (40-55 tons) at Regular-to-Veteran quality held back to strike once the sweep flushes out the pilot or the rescuers. The search homes on the pilot's beacon.
opforSketch.behavior: This force follows methodical search-and-cordon doctrine: advance the sweep in a steady, tightening line homing on the pilot's beacon, form a cordon on the likely exit to catch anyone the sweep flushes out, and hold the mobile strike force back to hit the pilot or the recovery team once located. The search does not rush — it relies on the steady shrinking of the net — but the strike element commits hard and fast the moment the sweep makes contact, prioritizing the capture of the pilot or the destruction of the recovery team over holding any ground. The sweep tightens relentlessly; the strike force breaks off only if the recovery team escapes the net entirely.

forks.name: OPERATION STAR ABOARD
forks.trigger: The pilot was reached ahead of the sweep and extracted through the closing net; the pilot and his knowledge are out.
forks.consequence: The pilot is out with what he knows and what his fighter recorded, denied to the occupiers who searched the ground for him. The order now is to act on the intelligence he brought home. Launch a follow-on strike shaped by what the pilot saw before he went down. Hit it before the occupier realizes the rescue worked and changes whatever the pilot's knowledge exposed. The pilot is aboard. Now what he saw gets put to use.

forks.name: OPERATION CLOSED NET
forks.trigger: The sweep reached the pilot first, or the recovery team was boxed in against the cordon; the pilot was captured or the rescue is trapped in the net.
forks.consequence: The search closed faster than the rescue. Either the sweep took the pilot, or the recovery team is boxed in against the cordon with the net tightening around it. The next operation is to break the team clear before it shares the pilot's fate. If the pilot was captured, plan his recovery from custody before he is moved to interrogation. The net closed. The rescuers become the rescued.

storyElementSeed: A recovery 'Mech pushes through wet jungle toward a beacon's pulse. Its pilot listens to the same signal the enemy is following. She watches the gaps in the canopy for the line of searchers she knows is somewhere ahead. They are closing on the injured man at the center from the other side.

is-davion.objectives.primary: Get to the downed pilot before the search does, take him aboard, and bring him out through the closing net. The beacon leads you both to him. Reach him first, or the rescue turns into having to take him back from the enemy.

is-steiner.objectives.primary: Reach the downed pilot ahead of the enemy search and extract him through the tightening sweep and cordon. The pilot and what he knows are the asset. Recover both before the search closes the net and the rescue costs more than the loss would.

COMB_TIGHTEN_HOURS.unit: hours for the comb to close

SURVIVOR_PACE_KMH.unit: km/h the hurt flyer can move

inspiration: A cutting-out expedition: a raiding party boards a vessel at its moorings, overpowers the watch, and sails it out from under the guns of the harbour before the defence can react — era-translated to seizing a grounded enemy DropShip at a field and flying it off, where the prize is taken away whole, the crew and codes to move it are the hard part, and a recall or a battery wakes the instant it lifts.
skeleton: a raiding party must seize an intact grounded enemy DropShip at a defended field and fly it off whole rather than destroy it, getting aboard, securing the bridge, and lifting on captured or coerced crew knowledge before the field's defences and a recall can stop it, where the prize must leave under its own power and undamaged so it cannot be fought over, the difficulty is in moving the ship not in taking the ground, and the field's battery and a recall code wake the instant it tries to lift, so the crux is the cutting-out and the getaway under power rather than a raid to wreck
title: OPERATION CUT LOOSE
situation: There is a working DropShip sitting on a field in {DISTRICT} on {WORLD}. {EMPLOYER} does not want it destroyed. It wants it stolen. The occupier has this grounded enemy DropShip at a secondary field. It is an intact hull, and the SLDF needs it far more than it needs another wreck. Lift capacity is scarce lostech, so a ship flown out whole is worth a campaign's worth of salvage. So the order is a boarding-and-theft raid. Get a party aboard, seize the bridge, and fly the ship off before the field's defenses can stop it. The prize has to leave under its own power and undamaged, and that is the hard part. You cannot fight over a ship you mean to keep, and you cannot blast your way aboard a hull you need spaceworthy. {NPC:intel-source} has the field, the ship's berth, and the guard rotation. There is one critical detail: your raiders cannot simply fly the ship themselves. Lifting her needs her own crew's knowledge, meaning the drive codes, the field clearance, and the launch sequence. So the plan depends on capturing or forcing enough of the ship's crew to move her. The intel on which crew are aboard and which sleep off-ship is {INTEL_AGE_HOURS} hours old. The trap waits at the lift. The instant the ship powers up to launch, the field knows. {NPC:opfor-commander} holds the field with a garrison. More dangerous is a ground battery set to fire on any ship trying to lift without clearance. There is also a recall protocol that can lock the ship's drives if the correct codes are not entered. The ground around the field is open and flat. It is fast going with no cover, so an alerted garrison crosses it quickly. Recommended force: {FORCE_SIZE}, a boarding party with enough combat strength to hold the field for the few minutes the lift takes. Get aboard quietly, seize the bridge and the crew who can fly her, and lift her off before the battery and the recall can stop the launch. Wreck her and you have a destroyed ship, not a stolen one. Alert the field before she lifts and she never leaves the ground.

objectives.primary: Board the grounded DropShip and secure the bridge and enough of her crew to fly her. Then lift the intact ship off the field before the garrison, the ground battery, and the recall protocol can stop the launch.
objectives.secondary: Take the ship undamaged and flyable. A holed hull, or a drive locked by the recall, is a ship that cannot leave. That turns the theft into a wreck your raid can use no better than the enemy could.
objectives.bonus: Lift the ship's cargo or the units aboard her along with the ship. A DropShip flown out loaded is the prize doubled; one flown out empty is just the hull.

complications.name: She Needs Her Crew to Fly
complications.text: Your raiders cannot simply walk onto the bridge and fly off. Moving the ship needs her own crew's knowledge: the drive codes, the launch sequence, the field clearance. So you must capture or force enough of the crew to fly her, alive and cooperating. A boarding that kills the wrong people, or finds the key crew asleep off-ship, is a boarding that took a hull it cannot move.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Lifting the ship needs specific crew, from the bridge and engineering, taken alive and cooperative. The raid must capture them, not just the ship. Crew killed during the boarding, or absent off-ship, cut the chance of a successful lift. A ship taken without enough crew knowledge cannot launch, so it fails the primary objective even with the hull held.

complications.name: Take Her Whole
complications.text: The prize is the intact ship, so the boarding must be careful where a raid would normally be brutal. Holing the hull, wrecking a drive, or burning the bridge all ground the ship the raid came to fly. The party cannot fight aboard the way it would on open ground. It has to take the ship without breaking it.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Damage to the ship during the boarding, whether to hull, drives, or bridge, hurts or prevents the lift. The prize must be taken intact. The boarding party is barred from using heavy weapons aboard the hull. That trades the ease of a brutal clearance against keeping the ship flyable.

complications.name: The Lift Is the Alarm
complications.text: A boarding might be done quietly, but a launch cannot. The instant the ship powers up her drives to lift, the field knows — there is no quiet way to fly a DropShip off a defended field. The whole garrison and the ground battery react to a ship lifting without clearance, and the recall protocol may lock the drives if the codes are wrong. The quiet part of the mission ends at the lift.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Powering the ship up to launch triggers the field's full response: the garrison alerts, the ground battery fires, and the recall protocol checks the codes the raiders entered. The withdrawal clock and the battery threat begin at the lift, not at the boarding. The lift itself is the trigger you must beat.

complications.name: The Battery and the Recall
complications.text: {NPC:opfor-commander} keeps a ground battery set to fire on a ship lifting without clearance. A DropShip is slowest and most vulnerable in the first seconds of a lift, and the battery is there for exactly that moment. A recall protocol can also lock the drives if the correct codes are not entered. So even a crew forced into flying may find the ship obeying its rightful owner's lockout instead.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The ground battery fires on the lifting ship during its vulnerable launch phase. Suppressing or destroying it before the lift removes the gravest threat to the getaway. The recall protocol may lock the drives unless the correct codes are entered, and those codes come from the crew. Wrong or missing codes can ground the ship at the moment of launch, even with the crew aboard.

decisionPoints.name: How to Cut Her Loose
decisionPoints.context: The ship has to be boarded, crewed, and lifted past the battery. The choice is how to approach the theft. Option one: board quietly and take the crew by surprise, to get her flying before the field reacts. Option two: take the battery first, so the lift is safe even if the boarding turns loud. Option three: seize the crew's off-ship billets first, to secure the codes before you ever board the hull.

options.title: Board Quiet, Lift Fast
advantages: A quiet boarding takes the crew by surprise and may have the ship powering up before the field is fully alerted
Gets the prize moving fastest — the lift underway before the garrison and battery can react
disadvantages: If the quiet boarding fails to secure the right crew or the codes, the ship cannot lift and the raid is aboard a hull it cannot move
The lift still alerts the battery, and a fast launch may go before the battery is suppressed
options.consequence: You get the ship moving fastest by boarding quietly and lifting hard. But you bet the launch on having the crew and codes in hand, and you lift under a battery that is still firing. It is the quickest getaway with the gravest threat unsuppressed.

costs.resource: the lift made fast under a battery not yet suppressed
costs.risk: A fast lift under a live battery means a ship hit in its vulnerable launch phase. Or a quiet boarding that lacked the crew and codes and cannot lift at all

options.title: Take the Battery First
advantages: Suppressing or destroying the ground battery first makes the lift safe even if the boarding turns loud
Removes the gravest threat to the getaway before the ship is committed to her vulnerable launch
disadvantages: Hitting the battery first is loud and alerts the field before the boarding — the crew may be warned and the bridge defended
An alerted crew may lock the ship down or destroy the codes before the boarding party reaches the bridge
options.consequence: You make the lift safe by destroying the battery first, but the noise alerts the field and the crew before you are aboard. The getaway is unthreatened, but the boarding is harder against a ship now defended and a crew now warned.

costs.resource: the surprise of the boarding spent alerting the field in order to destroy the battery first
costs.risk: Hitting the battery first warns the crew. An alerted crew locks the ship or destroys the codes before the boarding reaches the bridge. The lift is safe, but the ship is unflyable

options.title: Seize the Crew Billets First
advantages: Taking the key crew from their off-ship billets secures the codes and the knowledge before the hull is ever boarded
Guarantees the raid has what it needs to fly her, rather than gambling on finding it aboard
disadvantages: Hitting the billets is a separate action that alerts the field and the ship's watch before the boarding
Crew taken under duress may resist, mislead, or enter false codes at the lift
options.consequence: You make sure of the crew and codes by capturing them off-ship first, but the billet raid alerts the field and the ship's watch before you board. You have the means to fly her, but the ship herself is now alert and the crew unwilling.

costs.resource: the billet raid that secures the crew at the cost of alerting the field before the boarding
costs.risk: Forced crew may mislead you or enter false codes at the lift, and the billet raid warns the ship's watch. You have the codes in hand, but the boarding is harder for it

entries.event: The boarding party reaches the field and the ship's berth; the guard rotation and crew disposition are confirmed against the {INTEL_AGE_HOURS}-hour-old report.
The party gets aboard and moves on the bridge and the key crew; the boarding is underway, quiet if surprise holds.
The bridge and the crew who can fly her are secured. The ship begins powering up to lift, and the lift alerts the field, the battery, and the recall protocol.
The ship lifts through her vulnerable launch phase under the battery's fire and the recall check; {NPC:opfor-commander}'s garrison rushes the field.
The ship is up and away, clear of the battery's range, or she is grounded — locked by the recall, hit by the battery, or held by a garrison that reached the field first.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: The ship must be boarded, crewed, and lifted clear of the ground battery's range and the recall lock by around T+14:00. A lift under a live battery means a ship hit in her vulnerable launch phase. A recall locking the drives grounds her at the moment of launch. A garrison that reaches the field before she lifts holds the prize on the ground. Either way, the theft became a wreck or a siege.

opforSketch.composition: A field garrison plus an anti-lift battery: the field is held by a security garrison with a light-to-medium 'Mech section (25-50 tons) at Regular quality and motorized infantry, with the ship's own armed watch aboard. The decisive defensive element is a ground battery — fixed heavy guns positioned to fire on a DropShip in its vulnerable launch phase — plus {NPC:opfor-commander}'s mobile reaction force of medium 'Mechs (40-55 tons) and an armor section (Vedettes and Goblins) that rushes the field on the lift. A recall protocol can lock the ship's drives.
opforSketch.behavior: This force follows field-and-asset defense doctrine: the garrison holds the field and the ship's watch holds the hull, both alert to a boarding but counting on the lift being impossible to hide. The moment the ship powers up, the response is immediate — the ground battery fires on the lifting ship at her most vulnerable, the reaction force rushes the berth, and the recall protocol attempts to lock the drives. The battery fights above all to ground the ship during her launch phase; the reaction force presses to retake the berth or the ship before she clears. The defense prioritizes keeping the ship on the ground — intact or wrecked — over its own losses.

forks.name: OPERATION PRIZE CREW
forks.trigger: The ship was boarded, crewed, and lifted intact clear of the battery and the recall; the DropShip is flown off whole.
forks.consequence: The ship is up and away. It is an intact hull stolen from under the occupier's guns, worth a campaign's salvage to a lift-starved SLDF. The order now is to get the prize and her crew to safety before the occupier can launch a pursuit. That means a covered transit out of the system, in a ship the raiders can barely fly and the enemy badly wants back. The ship is taken. Now she is brought home.

forks.name: OPERATION DEAD WEIGHT
forks.trigger: The lift was stopped — the recall locked the drives, the battery grounded her, or the garrison retook the berth — and the ship is held on the field with the boarding party aboard or pinned.
forks.consequence: The theft failed at the lift. The ship is grounded by the recall or the battery, or the garrison is back on the berth, and the boarding party is stuck aboard a hull that will not fly as the field closes in. The next operation is to break the party clear of the grounded ship and the field. With the prize lost, you must also decide whether to wreck the ship you could not steal rather than leave it for the enemy. The prize is lost. The party gets out.

storyElementSeed: On a darkened DropShip bridge, a raider holds a sidearm on a captured flight officer. He tells the man to enter the launch sequence. He watches the man's hands move over the console. He has no way to know, until the drives light, whether the codes being keyed will fly her or lock her to the ground for good.

is-davion.objectives.primary: Board her, take the bridge and the crew who can fly her, and lift her off whole before the battery and the recall can stop it. We need the ship, not a wreck. Take her clean and fly her out, codes and all.

is-steiner.objectives.primary: Seize the grounded DropShip intact, secure the crew needed to move her, and lift her clear of the battery and the recall lock. Lift capacity is worth a campaign on the books. Bring the hull home flying, not as wreckage left on the field.

CREW_NEEDED.unit: key crew needed to fly her

inspiration: A signals-collection mission by physical tap: a small team infiltrates to an enemy command landline, splices a covert tap, and sits on it to harvest the order of battle, where the value of the intelligence rises the longer the tap runs but so does the chance the counter-intelligence loop sweeping the lines finds it, so the whole mission is the gamble of dwell against discovery.
skeleton: a small signals team must infiltrate to an enemy command landline trunk, emplace a covert physical tap, and remain on it harvesting the order of battle, where the intelligence value accrues with every day the tap runs but the chance a counter-intelligence line-sweep discovers it rises with the same dwell, the team must lie up undetected near the tap rather than fight, and the prize is the accumulated collection carried out clean, so the crux is the sliding gamble of how long to sit on the wire against the rising odds of being found rather than any single objective
title: OPERATION LONG WIRE
situation: The occupier's secrets on {WORLD} run down a buried wire, and {EMPLOYER} wants a team sitting on it. The Amaris command in {DISTRICT} routes its sensitive sector traffic by landline, not by radio. It does this because a buried cable cannot be intercepted from orbit. So the only way to read it is to reach it and tap it on the ground. That is the order. Infiltrate a signals team to the command cable, splice in a hidden physical tap, and stay on it. You will collect the sector's order of battle straight off the enemy's own wire. That means the unit positions, the reinforcement plans, and the chain of command. This is not a strike. It is a long stakeout. {NPC:intel-source} has the cable's route, the access point where it can be reached, and a nearby hiding place to wait in. But the read on enemy counter-intelligence activity is {INTEL_AGE_DAYS} days old, and the whole gamble of the mission turns on that activity. The longer the tap runs, the more it is worth. One day on the wire gives a snapshot. A week lays the whole sector bare. But the longer it runs, the more likely it is found. Amaris counter-intelligence sweeps its own lines for exactly this kind of tap. Its people physically walk the cables, check the signal, and hunt for any splice. Every day the team sits on the wire is another day for that sweep to come down the line. The team must stay hidden near the tap the whole time and must not fight. This is a signals stakeout deep in occupied territory. You collect until the value peaks or the sweep gets close, then carry the take out clean. {NPC:opfor-commander} runs the sector's security and the line-sweep. This commander also holds a mobile element ready to strike if the sweep flushes out the tap or the team. The terrain is broken and close. It is good ground for hiding a tap and a team, and good ground for a sweep to work unseen. Recommended force: {FORCE_SIZE}, a signals team with a light security element. Get on the wire, collect the sector, and know when to come off before the sweep finds the splice. Come off too early and you carry only a snapshot. Sit too long and the sweep takes you.

objectives.primary: Infiltrate to the command cable, install a hidden tap, and collect the sector's order of battle off the wire. Then carry the take out clean before the counter-intelligence sweep finds the tap or the team.
objectives.secondary: Stay hidden the entire time. The stakeout is blown the moment the team is seen. A tap found while the team is still on it loses both the intelligence and the team, not just the wire.
objectives.bonus: Wire the tap to feed a hidden device the team can leave behind and monitor from a distance. A normal stakeout ends when the team withdraws. This one keeps collecting after they are gone, until the sweep finds it.

complications.name: Dwell Against Discovery
complications.text: The mission is one sliding gamble. The intelligence is worth more the longer the tap runs. But the tap is also more likely to be found the longer it runs. One day gives a snapshot. A week gives the whole sector. Every extra day is another roll of the dice against the sweep coming down the line. There is no objective to seize, only the call of when the rising value beats the rising risk.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Track an accumulating intelligence value and a rising chance of discovery, both growing with each day the tap runs. The mission's payoff is the intelligence carried out before discovery; withdrawing early banks less, staying longer banks more but at a rising chance of losing it all. The decision is continuous, not a single point.

complications.name: The Line-Sweep
complications.text: Amaris counter-intelligence physically walks its own cables hunting for taps — checking the line's signal, inspecting the access points, and working down the wire toward any anomaly. The team cannot see the sweep coming until it is close, and a splice found is a splice the sweep traces back to the hiding place. The stakeout is a race the team runs blind against a hunter on the same wire.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The counter-intelligence sweep advances along the cable on its own schedule toward the tap. The team can only partly tell how close it is. When the sweep reaches the tap, it finds the splice and traces it toward the hiding place, which triggers the strike force. So the team must come off the wire before the sweep arrives.

complications.name: Lie Up, Do Not Fight
complications.text: The team's safety lies in appearing not to be there at all. It has to stay hidden near the tap the entire time, silent and still, because a stakeout that fights is a stakeout discovered. The light security element exists to break contact and cover a withdrawal, not to hold ground — the moment the team trades fire, the tap and the intelligence are blown.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The team must stay undetected the entire time. Any contact or firefight blows the stakeout. It ends the collection and triggers the strike force, no matter where the discovery clock stands. The security element can cover a withdrawal but cannot fight to stay on the wire. A firefight means the stakeout has failed, not that it is being defended.

complications.name: Broken, Close Country
complications.text: The cable runs through broken, close terrain — ridges and timber that hide the tap and the team's hiding place, and also hide the sweep working toward them. The cover that conceals the team conceals the hunter, and the slow going that protects the team's approach slows its withdrawal when the sweep finally comes close.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The close terrain conceals the team and the sweep alike and slows movement; the hiding place is well-concealed but the sweep can approach unseen. The slow going lengthens the withdrawal once the team decides to come off the wire, narrowing the margin between deciding to leave and the sweep arriving.

decisionPoints.name: How Long to Sit the Wire
decisionPoints.context: The tap is running, the intelligence is building, and the sweep is somewhere down the line. The gamble is how long to stay. Option one: come off early with a solid snapshot, banking a sure but smaller prize. Option two: stay on the wire for the whole sector, betting the rising value against the approaching sweep. Option three: splice in a hidden leave-behind device and withdraw, then collect from a distance until the sweep finds the tap with no team on it.

options.title: Come Off Early, Bank the Snapshot
advantages: Carries out a solid snapshot of the sector with the team clear and the intelligence safe
Comes off the wire well before the sweep can close in — the lowest risk of losing the team or the take
disadvantages: A short stay banks a snapshot, not the whole sector — the deeper intelligence a longer stakeout would yield is left on the wire
The tap is pulled while it was still producing, cutting the mission's potential short for safety
options.consequence: You bank a sure, useful take and bring the team home clean. But you leave the deeper picture uncollected. You have the safe prize in hand, and the sector's secrets still run down a wire you walked away from.

costs.resource: the deeper intelligence left uncollected for the safety of an early withdrawal
costs.risk: An early withdrawal banks a snapshot when the whole sector was within reach. It is a sure small prize where a patient one was building

options.title: Ride It Long for the Sector
advantages: A long stay collects the whole sector — unit positions, plans, and chain of command laid bare off the enemy's wire
Banks the richest possible intelligence if the team comes off before the sweep arrives
disadvantages: Every extra day is another roll of the dice against the sweep finding the splice and tracing it to the hiding place
A stakeout held too long loses the team and all the gathered intelligence together when the sweep arrives
options.consequence: You go for the whole sector by sitting the wire a long time, and if you read the sweep right you carry out the richest take of the campaign. Misjudge it and the sweep finds the tap with the team still on it, and the whole stakeout is lost at once.

costs.resource: the rising odds of discovery accepted in order to collect the whole sector
costs.risk: A stakeout held too long is found with the team still on it. The richest intelligence and the team are lost together when the sweep arrives

options.title: Leave a Relay, Harvest from Afar
advantages: A leave-behind device keeps the tap collecting after the team withdraws, giving the value of a long stay without the team's continued exposure
Lets the intelligence keep building from a safe distance until the sweep eventually finds the unmanned tap
disadvantages: Splicing in and concealing such a device takes more time on the wire up front and is a more complex, more findable installation
If the device is found, the intelligence is lost without warning, and its take must still be retrieved or transmitted, each its own risk
